# Fransys 0.19.8

> The whole guide, the part-file contracts and the API pages in one file.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/index.md -->

# Fransys

Fransys is a Python toolkit for authoring electrical cabinet and harness designs and
producing their schematics, parts lists and manufacturing exports from one model. This page
lists every consumer task with its one spelling, then the install and the shape of a script.

Fransys is in Beta: the API may change between minor versions until 1.0.0, and each release's guide says what changed.

## The public surface

The public surface has four parts: `fr.__all__`, `fr.derive.__all__`, `fransys.colours`, and every keyword of every public call and every `d.*` method, with the `d.layout.profile` keywords and the `d.layout.sheet` numbers. Nothing else is public, and every part has an entry in this guide.

## Tiers

Every `fr.*` function and handle method opens its docstring with one of four tier words.

- `Core:` the calls a project is written with.
- `Detail:` a call for a case no core call writes; its docstring names the core call to try first.
- `Read:` reads a built model or a part library and changes nothing.
- `Output:` builds, checks, reports, writes or releases.

A namespace sets the tier of the names under it, so they carry no word: `d.*` is core, `d.detail.*` and `d.layout.*` are detail, and `fr.derive.*` is read.
Types, constants, colours and exceptions have no tier.

## Which call first

Write a design with the core calls below. They pair poles, take the next free terminal or core,
and give layout the structure it draws. The detail calls in the table are for their cases only
(detail.md).

1. A cabinet or a board is a unit: `@fr.unit`, then `d.add` (units.md).
2. Name places with `d.location`. Put each circuit in its own block, `with d.function(tag, text):`.
3. Declare every supply with `d.dc_supply` or `d.ac_supply`. Start and end each path on its rails.
4. Write each current path as one `d.series(...)`, source first. Devices, functions, rails, strips,
   runs and cables are its elements.
5. A branch between two neighbours is a `d.parallel(...)` element. A branch across several
   elements is a second series, from the split to the join.
6. Pass a strip, a run or a cable to the series. It takes the next free terminal or core, on the
   right side.
7. Bridge with `bridged=` on the strip or the run. Request a PLC signal on its function,
   `K1.coil.plc(fr.DO, name)`, and pass the PLC module whole to the series: it takes its lowest
   free channel (authoring.md, how channels are numbered).
8. A circuit that repeats is a Python function around these calls, fed by a table (examples.md).
9. Add `d.layout.*` advice last, only where the structure leaves the drawing a choice.

| detail call | only for |
|---|---|
| `d.detail.wire(a, b, wire=...)` | two named pins off any path, such as a signal pair; one signal daisy-chained, `d.detail.wire(a, b, c)`; a hop whose printed wire differs from its row |
| `X1[3]`, `.inner`, `.outer` | a terminal whose number or side is fixed: a published pinout, or several wires on one terminal |
| `W1.core(BN, a, b)` | a core whose colour or number a termination plan fixes |
| `d.detail.net(name, *pins)` | a named net that no wire joins, such as a bus shown by its label |
| `d.detail.busbar(a, b)`, `d.detail.rail_bond(a, b)` | a rack's internal jumper; terminals bonded through their rail |

`d.series` raises `has no pole pair: its part states no line side` when a part does not say which pin is the line
side. Fix the part file (`side = "line"`, parts.md), or wire the pins with `d.detail.wire`. A real circuit that no
core call can write is a gap in Fransys: report it with its smallest shape.

## Tasks

Each task has one spelling. `P` is a generated parts module or an MPN string; `BU` and `BN` come
from `fransys.colours`.

| task | its one spelling | where it is taught |
|---|---|---|
| load a library, start a design | `d = fr.design("demo_parts")` | parts.md, Loading a library |
| load a library, no design | `fr.parts(*names)` | parts.md |
| lint a library | `fr.lint(*names)` | parts.md, Linting a library |
| name a place | `d.location("HOLD", text)`, then `place="HOLD"` | authoring.md, name a place |
| name a function block | `with d.function("M1", text):` | authoring.md, name a function block |
| add a device | `d.device("Q1", P.X, place=, parent=, mounted_on=, joins=)` | authoring.md, add a device |
| read a function or pin | `Q1.coil`, `Q1["A1"]`, `Q1[2]` | authoring.md, read a function or pin |
| add a terminal strip, take a terminal | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.X, n)`, `X1[3]` | authoring.md, Strips and terminals |
| a named, bridged run on a strip | `X1.run(label, n, bridged=True)` | authoring.md, Bridges |
| bridge a set of auto-numbered terminals | `X1.run(label, bridged=True)`, then the run passed to each `d.series` | authoring.md, Bridges |
| wire along a current path | `d.series(a, b, c, wire=(BU, 0.75))` | authoring.md, wire along a current path |
| branch inside a series | `d.parallel(a, b)` | authoring.md, branch inside a series |
| a branch across part of a path | a second `d.series(split, ..., join, wire=...)` | authoring.md, Branch inside a series |
| a series from one pin, or a branch looped at a fuse's line pins | `d.series(k1.coil["A1"], a1.di_1)`, `d.series((f4.element[1], f4.element[3], f4.element[5]), f8.element)` | keywords-handles.md |
| bridge adjacent plain terminals | `d.terminal_strip("X4", P.X, 6, bridged=(2, 6))` | authoring.md, Bridges |
| wire one point to many | `d.detail.star(src, (a, b, c), wire=...)` | detail.md, One point to many |
| wire two named pins off a path | `d.detail.wire(a, b, wire=(BU, 0.75))` | detail.md, d.detail.wire |
| add a cable | `d.cable("W1", P.X, length_m=)` in a `d.series`, which takes the next free core | authoring.md, Cables |
| a signal pair through a cable, pin for pin | `d.pair(a, cable, b)` | keywords-design.md, d.pair |
| choose one core of a cable | `W1.core(BN, a, b)` | detail.md, W1.core |
| name a wire colour | `from fransys.colours import BU`, then `wire=(BU, 0.75)` | authoring.md, Wire colours |
| colour wires by what they carry | `fr.design(..., wiring=)`, `@fr.unit(wiring=)` or `wire={row: ...}` | authoring.md, Wire colours |
| a changeover throw in a series | `k1.co_1.no`, `.nc` | authoring.md, A changeover in a series |
| earth pins | `d.earth(*pins)` | authoring.md, earth pins |
| a named signal net | `d.detail.net(name, *pins, kind=)` | detail.md |
| a busbar, a rail bond | `d.detail.busbar(a, b)`, `d.detail.rail_bond(a, b)` | detail.md |
| AC or DC supply and rails | `d.ac_supply(...)`, `d.dc_supply(...)` | authoring.md, AC or DC supply and rails |
| name a place inside a place | `d.location("BATT", text, within="HOLD")` | authoring.md, A place inside a place |
| take one pole of a multi-pole function | `s1.main.pole(2)` | keywords-handles.md, Fn.pole |
| list a function's pins in order | `fn.pins` | detail.md, W1.core |
| plug a connector | `d.mate(a, b)` | authoring.md, plug a connector |
| add a harness | `d.harness("W5")` | harnesses.md, add a harness |
| group PLC modules in a rack | `d.rack` | authoring.md |
| request a PLC channel, scale it | `K1.coil.plc(fr.DO, name)`, `.scale(...)` | authoring.md, request a PLC channel |
| wire a path to a PLC channel | `d.series(dc.plus, s1.no, a1)`; fixed: `a1.di_7` | authoring.md, how channels are numbered |
| title block, revision | `d.project(...)`, `d.revision(...)` | authoring.md, title block, revision |
| read a part's rating while authoring | `d.rating(part, fn)`, `d.operating(part, fn)` | parts.md, Reading a part's rating while authoring |
| advise the drawing | `d.layout.chain`, `keep_together`, `break_before`, `order`, `symbol`, `draw_in`, `side`, `sheet`, `profile` | detail.md, Layout profile |
| put a unit's interface above or below its outline | `d.layout.side(u1.bus_in, fr.ABOVE)`, `fr.BELOW` | detail.md, Layout profile |
| define a unit | `@fr.unit(name, revision=, interface_version=, ...)` | units.md, define a unit |
| add a unit instance, reach its boundary | `d.add(fn, "U1")` returns the unit's `NamedTuple`, `io.X1` | units.md, Nesting units |
| mark some terminals of a strip a unit boundary | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.X, 4, interface=(1, 2))`, `unused=` the same | units.md, The boundary |
| mark a boundary device | `interface=True`, `unused=True` on `d.device` | units.md, The boundary |
| leave one placed instance's boundary open | `d.add(fn, "U2", unused=("X1",))` | units.md, Leaving one instance open |
| state a boundary's values | `X1.power.limits(rating=, operating=)` | units.md, The boundary |
| build the model | `fr.build(d, *documents)` | build.md |
| add a document | `fr.document(preset, subject, cover=)` | documents.md |
| all findings of a build | `fr.check(result)` | build.md, `fr.check` sees more |
| a readable report of them | `fr.report(result)` | build.md, `fr.report` |
| write exports | `fr.write(result, out_dir)` | build.md |
| the name of each export | `fr.export_names(result, unit=None)` | build.md, Export file names |
| release a baseline | `fr.release(result, into)` | build.md, Releasing |
| list changes since a release | `fr.diff(result, baselines)` | build.md, Getting the change list |
| test a baseline stays true | `fr.verify(result, baselines)` | build.md, Checking a baseline |
| list the releases on disk | `fr.releases(root)` | build.md, Listing the releases |
| read a built model | `fr.derive.<function>(model, ...)` | reading.md |
| an easy and an efficient level | same calls, a function or a loop around them | examples.md, easy and efficient |

## Install

Fransys is not on PyPI yet. Pin it as a git dependency, at a release tag:

```toml
[project]
dependencies = [
    "fransys @ git+https://github.com/OleJBondahl/fransys@vX.Y.Z#subdirectory=packages/fransys",
]
```

Replace `vX.Y.Z` with the release you pin.

## The shape of a build script

A script starts a design from an installed part library (`fr.design`), authors it with
`d.device` and wiring, adds a cabinet as a unit (`@fr.unit`, `d.add`), and passes the design to
`fr.build`, which merges and freezes a model and lays out the schematic when a document keeps a SCHEMATIC page. `fr.check` collects every finding about the built model;
`fr.write` writes the exports to a directory, raising instead of writing anything if `check`
found an `ERROR`. A design with no document has nothing to draw, so `build` still succeeds and
`write` still produces the parts-list exports.

```python
from pathlib import Path
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit("pump-cabinet", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="First", by="AB")
def cabinet(c):
    c.device("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")

result = fr.build(d)  # no document: no layout
print(fr.report(result))  # the summary, each error and warning with its fix, then the notes
findings = fr.check(result)
assert not [f for f in findings if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
fr.write(result, Path("out"))
```

`fr.report(result)` prints what the build found, so a script shows its warnings on every run.

## The rest of this guide

### Writing a project

- `parts.md`: loading and linting a part library, the typed parts module, and a part's rating.
- `authoring.md`: places, functions, devices, strips, series, cables, colours and supplies.
- `units.md`: a unit's boundary, its revisions, and nesting one unit inside another.
- `harnesses.md`: adding a harness, and how its cables and plugs print.
- `documents.md`: presets, covers, subjects, and one PDF per drawing.
- `build.md`: `build`, `check`, `write`, `release`, `verify`, and where each can fail.
- `examples.md`: worked examples, and a pointer to a full build script.
- `examples/demo-skid/skid.py`, outside the guide: a whole skid cabinet on demo parts, as a worked design of high-level calls (its README says how to build it).

### Detail and edge cases

- `detail.md`: each `d.detail` call, `W1.core`, fixed terminals and `d.layout` advice, with the cases they are for.
- `drawing.md`: what layout reads, a checklist for a readable cabinet, printed sizes and grid pitch.
- `layout-numbers.md`: every `d.layout.profile` keyword and every `d.layout.sheet` number.
- `readability.md`: `fr.readability`, the per-page and per-unit numbers behind the readability findings.

### Reading a built model

- `reading.md`: reading a built model back: tables, rows, designations and ratings.
- `reading-rows.md`: the column constants, row types, row functions and printed texts of `fr.derive`.
- `reading-records.md`: the record types, lookups and ratings of `fr.derive`.
- `overview.md`: reading the system overview page `write` makes.

### Findings

- `findings.md`: every finding code, what it means and the usual fix, on five pages by source: `findings-validators.md`, `findings-render.md`, `findings-pdf.md`, `findings-kicad.md` and `findings-parts.md`.

### Reference

- `keywords.md`: the signal types, handles, `Severity` and the keywords of the record constructors.
- `keywords-design.md`, `keywords-handles.md` and `keywords-output.md`: one table for each public call, with each keyword's default, effect and an example.
- `kicad.md`: importing a board netlist into KiCad, with the settings to use.

### Moving from an older release

- `moving-to-0.19.md`: the detail calls that moved to `d.detail`, and the rewrite from `d.wire` to `d.series`.
- `moving-to-0.16-and-0.17.md`: what may newly stop a 0.15 or 0.16 build, the changed outputs and the new names.
- `moving-to-0.15.md`: each renamed profile and readability name, the new `releases=` keyword and the system overview's Changes switch.
- `moving-to-0.14.md`: every `fr.derive` name 0.14 removes, and what to use instead.
- `moving-to-0.6.md`: each break from 0.5, with the old spelling, the new one and why.
- `moving-to-fransys.md`: the alias, the pin line, the parts-module command and the intermediates folder for a 0.6.1 consumer of the old name.

# Parts

A part library is a Python data package: TOML files describing parts, and no code. Fransys
never reads a spreadsheet or a manufacturer's own format directly; every part your design
uses comes from an installed library written against the part-file contract. This page covers
starting a design from a library, the typed parts module, class codes, linting and load failures. The
contract itself is the "Part file contract" page of the site, at the version you
installed. Read it before you write a library.

## Starting a design

`fr.design` takes the import names of one or more installed part-data packages and returns a
design `d` with every part, function and port of those libraries loaded. A device names its
part by manufacturer part number (MPN), as a string. This is the data-driven path: the part
list can come from a table or a file.

```python
# easy: start a design
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
d.device("H2", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
```

A part is either a typed object from the generated parts module or an MPN string. That is one
argument of `d.device`, not two spellings of one task. Use the typed object when you write the
part by hand and want completion and checking, and the string when the MPN comes from data.
Two parts with one MPN from two makers have no spelling in this release.

## The typed parts module

The generator writes one Python module for a library: a class per part, with its functions and
pins as typed attributes. Your editor then completes `H1.lamp[1]` and flags a pin the part does
not have. Regenerate the module whenever the library changes. Run this from a shell:

```text
python -m fransys parts-module demo_parts demo_typed.py
```

`fr.parts_module("demo_parts")` returns the same module as text, when a script writes the file itself.

The part library generates this module and ships it, and the projects that use the library import it
rather than generate their own. A pin whose marking is not a Python name gets an attribute by the
one name rule (authoring.md): the pin `1/L1` is `k.main.P_1_L1` and `24V1` is `psu.P_24V1`, each checked by ty.
The pin is also `k.main["1/L1"]`. Pass `interface=` a tuple of the part's function names and a
misspelt name is a ty error.

The `part` argument of `d.device` is a string or a generated class. A string is checked when you
build. Two part names that map to one attribute fail generation, and so do two pins of one function.

A function stands in a `d.series` when its line side is known: a coil's A1 and a contact's odd pin give it, else state `side`.

A pin that sources a wiring row, such as a drive's `U`, `V` and `W` outputs, states it with `source_row = "AC_L1"` (any `WiringRow` name). A `d.series` wire from that pin then takes the row's colour without `wire=`.

The module records the library's digest. `fr.design(P, ...)` compares that digest with the
library it loads and raises an error naming the command above when the module is stale. A
whitespace edit in a part file is not stale; any changed fact is. The efficient level of the
task builds the same model with the typed module and a loop:

```python
# efficient: start a design
import subprocess
import sys

import fransys as fr

subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-m", "fransys", "parts-module", "demo_parts", "demo_typed.py"], check=True
)
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import demo_typed as P

d = fr.design(P)
for tag in ("H1", "H2"):
    d.device(tag, P.DEMO_LAMP_24)
```

## Class codes

A part's `class_code` seeds its printed designation (`-Q1`, `-Q2`). Recommended codes, IEC 81346-2:2019:

| Object | Code |
|---|---|
| Contactor, main switch, switch-disconnector | Q |
| Fuse, MCB (protection) | F |
| Relay, PLC coupler and modules, network switch | K |
| Overload relay, sensor, current transformer | B |
| Signal lamp, meter, display | P |
| Terminal, terminal strip | X |
| Plug, socket, board header (connector) | J |
| Power supply, transformer | T |
| Motor, solenoid actuator | M |
| Suppressor diode, resistor | R |
| Board (PCB), rack | U |
| Cable, harness | W |
| Heater | E |
| Push button, selector, emergency stop | S |

## Loading a library without a design

`fr.parts` takes the same import names and returns a single `Draft` holding every part,
function, port and facet record, each carrying the file and line it came from. Use it to lint a
library or build without a design:

```python
import fransys as fr

parts = fr.parts("demo_parts")
```

Loading several libraries together, as in `fr.design("a", "b")` or `fr.parts("a", "b")`,
merges them into one library.

## Linting a library

`fr.lint(*libraries)` checks one or more libraries against the part-file contract without
building a model: every part file's fields, enum values, port and link shapes, and the
cross-file rules (duplicate parts, duplicate connector labels, and so on), collected as
`Finding`s.

```python
findings = fr.lint("demo_parts")
assert not [f for f in findings if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
```

The argument is the library's import name, resolved exactly as `fr.parts` resolves it: an
installed package's own root, the directory that directly holds `library.toml`. For the demo
library that is `demo_parts`, the inner package, never `examples/demo-parts`, the outer
project folder that merely contains it (and holds the package's own `pyproject.toml`, not a
part file). Passing the project folder's name is the mistake to watch for. `fr.lint` and
`fr.parts` both want the package's own name, the same one you would give `uv add` or an
`import` statement.

## When a library fails to load

`fr.parts` runs the same checks `fr.lint` does before it builds anything, and refuses to load a
library that fails them: it raises `fr.PartLibraryError`, whose `findings` attribute holds
every finding lint collected, warnings included, not only the errors that caused the raise. So
does `fr.design`. A library with a genuine problem (a part file missing its required `[part]`
table, in this made-up example) never reaches your model:

```python
import sys
from pathlib import Path

Path("bad_parts/parts").mkdir(parents=True)
Path("bad_parts/__init__.py").write_text('"""A broken library, for this example only."""\n')
Path("bad_parts/library.toml").write_text(
    'schema = 1\nname = "bad-parts"\nversion = "0.0.1"\ndescription = "missing its [part] table"\n'
)
Path("bad_parts/parts/broken.toml").write_text("schema = 1\n")
sys.path.insert(0, ".")

try:
    fr.parts("bad_parts")
except fr.PartLibraryError as e:
    assert e.findings[0].code == "FIELD_MISSING"
else:
    raise AssertionError("expected PartLibraryError")
```

Catch `fr.PartLibraryError` around a load whose library you do not control yourself: one built
by a separate team or vendor. An uncaught `PartLibraryError` already stops your script right
there, with Python's own one-line traceback. Catching it instead gets you `e.findings`: every
finding the failed load collected, not only the one that raised, so you can report the library's
whole set of problems at once instead of fixing them one exception at a time.

## A contact a person or a machine operates

A push button, an emergency stop, a selector or a limit switch states what operates its
contacts in `[part]`: `operated_by = "push"`, `"mushroom"`, `"turn"` or `"position"`. Its
contacts are `switch` functions, and the drawing picks the symbol from the operator and the
rest state: a push button closed at rest draws `push-button-break`. A part that wants one
actuator over several contacts states one `switch` function per contact.

A complete device, such as a limit switch, states it on itself. A head sold apart from its
contact blocks states it and has no function. Each block holds one `switch` and joins the head
with `parent=`:

```python
s1 = d.device("S1", "DEMO-HEAD-ESTOP")
first = d.device(None, "DEMO-BLOCK-1NC", name="nc-1", parent=s1)
second = d.device(None, "DEMO-BLOCK-1NC-21", name="nc-2", parent=s1)
```

Both blocks print `-S1`, and each draws the emergency-stop symbol.
`d.layout.profile(actuator_each_contact=False)` draws one actuator per device: the first block,
11-12, draws the symbol and the list of both contacts; the second draws its break contact with a
reference to the first.

## Ratings from a datasheet

A part's rating fields are read straight off its datasheet, but a battery or cell datasheet
often states its rating as a C-rate against the part's capacity rather than as a current: 1C
on 310 Ah is 310 A. Do that multiplication yourself before writing the part file. A
`[function.operating]` table's `max_current_dc_a` is a current, in amps, never a C-rate.
Fransys stores whatever number you give it and does not compute this conversion.

A protective device's datasheet gives its breaking capacity as points: the voltage, the current it breaks there
and, for DC, the circuit's time constant. A part states them in `[rating]` or `[function.rating]` as `breaking_ac` and
`breaking_dc`. A source's datasheet gives its fault current and time constant in `[function.operating]`.

```toml
# a DC fuse function
[function.rating]
voltage_dc_v = "1000"
current_dc_a = "125"
breaking_dc = [{ voltage_v = "1000", current_a = "15000", time_constant_ms = "15" }]

# a battery function
[function.operating]
nominal_voltage_v = "51.2"
fault_current_dc_a = "6000"
fault_time_constant_ms = "2"
```

A replaceable part, such as a fuse link in its holder, is its own part file. It states a top-level
`[rating]` and has no `[[function]]`. The holder keeps the pads and the footprint.

```toml
[part]
mpn = "DEMO-FUSE-LINK-4A-T"
manufacturer = "Demo"
description = "Replaceable fuse link for a PCB holder, 4 A time-lag, 1000 V DC"
category = "protection"
class_code = "F"

[rating]
voltage_dc_v = "1000"
current_dc_a = "4"
```

`d.rating("DEMO-FUSE-LINK-4A-T")` reads that rating. Put the link in its holder with `parent=`, as `authoring.md`
shows. A link with `min_breaking_current_a` is partial-range and bounds no current.

```python
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
rating = d.rating("DEMO-FUSE-LINK-4A-T")
assert rating is not None and rating.current_dc_a == 4
```

## Reading a part's rating while authoring

`d.rating(part, function)` and `d.operating(part, function)` read a rating or operating envelope
from the catalogue. It is a lookup, not a build step. Either gives `None` where the part states nothing.

```python
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
part_rating = d.rating("DEMO-TBLK-2P-DUAL")
terminal_rating = d.rating("DEMO-TBLK-2P-DUAL", "terminal")
lamp_operating = d.operating("DEMO-LAMP-24", "lamp")
```

## An accessory in its holder

A part with no function, put in another device with `parent=`, is an accessory. A fuse link in its PCB
holder is one: the link prints `F1` and has no number or row. An authored tag makes it an ordinary item.
`parent=` also takes a terminal strip, for a jumper bar on a bridged run.

```python
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
f1 = d.device("F1", "DEMO-FUSE-HOLDER-PCB")
link = d.device(None, "DEMO-FUSE-LINK-4A-T", name="link", parent=f1)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
x1.run("L", 3, bridged=True)
bar = d.device(None, "DEMO-JUMPER-BAR-3P", name="bar", parent=x1)
model = fr.build(d).model
assert fr.derive.item_designation(model, link.id) == "F1"
assert fr.derive.item_designation(model, bar.id) == "X1"
```

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/authoring/index.md -->

# Authoring a design

This page teaches how to write a design with `fr.design`: places, function blocks, devices, terminal
strips, wires, cables, supplies, PLC requests and layout advice. Each task has one spelling, shown
first written out and then with Python around it.

A `Design` is one object with no global state. Every call returns a handle, never a string, and later calls take it. A design is a draft: `fr.build(d)` freezes it (see `build.md`).

## Easy and efficient

Each task is shown twice and builds the same model both times. The easy level writes the circuit out,
one device and one wire per line. The efficient level uses the same calls with Python around them: a
loop over a table, a function for a circuit that repeats. Both use the same calls.

The pairs below are: a function block with devices, a branched series, and a terminal strip with a series.
The sections after them list the one-call tasks.

## Name a place and a function block

A place is where units and field devices stand: a room, a site, a ship's hold. `d.location("HOLD", text)`
names it, and `place="HOLD"` on `d.device` or `fr.design` puts devices there. A cabinet is not a place.
It is a unit that holds components, units and wires (see `units.md`). A function block is one circuit,
such as one pump's or one string's: `with d.function("LAMPS", text):` puts every device made inside it
in that block, and a circuit is never a place. Tags are bare: `"HOLD"`, never `"+HOLD"`, and a prefixed
tag raises.

What `place=` changes, on every call that takes it.

| value | effect |
|---|---|
| `...` (the default) | The item takes the design's place, the one `fr.design(place=)` named. With none named, it has no place. |
| `"HOLD"` | The item stands in that place. Its designation gains the prefix `+HOLD`, or `+HOLD+BATT` in a nested place. The place must exist. |
| `None` | The item has no place, even when the design names one. |

A place sorts the lists by place and sets the `+` part of the printed designation. It does not move a cell on a drawing: `d.layout.draw_in` does.

`d.device(tag, part, place=, parent=, mounted_on=, joins=, interface=, unused=, name=)` adds one device.
`joins={1: K1.coil["A1"]}` with `parent=K1` fits a housing on K1's own leads: pin 1 is that pin, no wire.
A contact block with `parent=` an operator head prints the head's tag, as `-S1:11` (guide `parts.md`).
`part` is a manufacturer part number such as `"DEMO-LAMP-24"`.

Floating tags: every item call takes `None` for the tag and numbers the item from its class code.
Pass `name=`, the identity a released number holds to; a floating call with no `name=` raises.
An accessory takes its holder's designation, no number of its own.

`external=True` marks an item supplied by others. Every call that makes an item takes it: `d.device`,
`d.terminal_strip`, `d.cable` and `d.harness`. The item has no BOM line. A strip's terminals are external
with it; a cable's conductors carry no flag. Every drawing marks it: dashed boxes with "(by others)", dashed outlines round schematic symbols.

An external device or strip may take `None` for its part, when only its terminal names are known. It needs a tag. A part-less device names its pins with `pins=`. A part-less strip offers only `.outer`: see `detail.md`, "Equipment others supply".

```python
# easy: function block
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
with d.function("RUN", "Pump run"):
    k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
    k2 = d.device("K2", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
    h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
    h2 = d.device("H2", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
    d.series(dc.plus, k1.aux, h1.lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
    d.series(dc.plus, k2.aux, h2.lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
```

```python
# efficient: function block
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

LAMPS = {"H1": "K1", "H2": "K2"}  # lamp tag -> the contactor whose auxiliary contact lights it

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
with d.function("RUN", "Pump run"):
    for tag, contactor in LAMPS.items():
        k = d.device(contactor, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
        lamp = d.device(tag, "DEMO-LAMP-24")
        d.series(dc.plus, k.aux, lamp.lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
```

`getattr(dev, f"DI{n}")` is the one spelling for a computed name. A name the device lacks raises an
error that `hasattr` reads as absent.

A device with one function and a marked pin is read the short way: `h1[1]`.

### A place inside a place

`d.location("BATT", text, within="HOLD")` puts the place `BATT` inside `HOLD`, named by its tag.
`HOLD` must exist already, or the call raises and lists the places. A device placed in `BATT`
prints `+HOLD+BATT`. Without `within=` a place sits at the root.

### Read a function or pin

A device has functions, and a function has pins. Both are plain attributes and brackets.

`Q1.coil` is a function by name, `Q1["A1"]` a pin by marking, and `Q1[2]` a pin by number. A name or
marking the part lacks raises and lists the choices. The vocabulary is the electrotechnical one: a
make contact closes when its coil is on, a break contact opens, a line conductor is `L1`.

A printed marking that is not a Python name has two spellings. `dev["XLA+"]` reaches any pin by its
printed marking. `dev.XLA_plus` reaches a function or a pin named `XLA+`: `+` gives `_plus`, `-` gives `_minus`,
any other non-word character `_`, and a leading digit gets `P_`, so `24V+` is `P_24V_plus` and the pin `1/L1`
is `P_1_L1`. `getattr(dev, "24V+")` reaches the raw name.

## Strips and terminals

`d.terminal_strip("X1", part, count, description=, pe=)` adds a terminal strip of `count` terminals,
and `X1[3]` takes terminal 3. `pe` names the protective-earth part, and a run labelled exactly `"PE"` (`X1.run("PE", 2)`) takes it; without `pe=` that run raises. A terminal has two sides: wiring
inside the unit reaches its inner side, a field cable its outer side. A wire or a series enters a
strip at the right side without you saying so.
A series that starts on a strip and goes on to a function leaves the strip on its inner side.
One that goes on to a cable leaves it on the outer side.

With `count`, the strip makes all its terminals at once, so spares exist and count in the lists. A
terminal joins the function block where it is first taken, and a spare joins the strip's own group.
There is no `group=` keyword. A series picks the side itself. `x1[1].outer` is
the field side, and `W1.core(...)` lands there. `d.series(x1[3].outer, f1.element)` pins the side.
A series of only fixed terminals takes its width from the first; one terminal is one pole.
A tuple takes one-terminal runs, `(x4.l1[1], x4.l2[1])`, and the colours of the net an earlier series made.
`interface=` and `unused=` on `d.terminal_strip` mark terminals a unit boundary: `True` marks every
terminal, and a tuple of numbers, `interface=(1, 2)`, only those; the others stay inside the unit. On
a run they take `True` only: `x1.run("24V", 4, bridged=True, interface=True)` (see `units.md`).

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
with d.function("FEED", "Lamp feed"):
    d.series(x1, h1.lamp, x1, wire=(BU, 0.75))
```

### Bridges

`X1.run(label, n, bridged=True)` takes `n` terminals as a named run, joined by jumpers when
`bridged=True`. A run's `bridged=` bridges a named run, and a strip's bridges plain terminals. Two terminals are a run of two.
Made inside a function block, a run puts all its terminals in that block. Made outside every block, it puts
none: each terminal joins the block it is first wired in.

`bridged=(first, last)` bridges terminals `first` to `last` only, one jumper between each
consecutive pair. A pair outside 1 to `n`, or with `first >= last`, raises and names the range.

A strip with a `count` bridges plain terminals with no run and no label:
`d.terminal_strip("X4", part, 6, bridged=(2, 6))` jumpers terminals 2 to 6, `bridged=((2, 3), (5, 6))`
makes two bridges, and `bridged=True` bridges them all. A bad range raises and names the fix.

`X1.run(label, bridged=True)` takes no size. The run grows as connections take its terminals, and
each new one is bridged to the one before. `feed[n]` names a terminal already taken; a higher `n`
raises. A strip or a run is also a core's end: each place takes its next free terminal, a series on the
inner side and `W1.core` on the outer side.

```python
# a growing bridged run fed by d.series
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
feed = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5").run("24V", bridged=True)
for tag in ("H1", "H2", "H3"):
    d.series(dc.plus, feed, d.device(tag, "DEMO-LAMP-24").lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
```

## Wiring and cables

`d.series` takes `wire=` in four shapes (Wire colours): a colour code and a cross-section in mm2,
a size, a table of rows, or a tuple of `(colour, mm2)`, one per pole.

### Wire along a current path

`d.series(a, b, c, wire=(BU, 0.75))` wires elements end to end: each one's load side to the next
one's line side, one wire per pole. A supply rail, a run, a device function, a cable and a strip
are all elements. A function is a series element when its part names its line side; else the
series raises and names it. A part-less external device may end a series: its pins meet the poles in
declared order; anywhere else it raises.

### Branch inside a series

`d.parallel(a, b)` is an element of a series: each member sits between the previous load and the next
line.

A branch across several elements is a second series, from the split to the join. Below, the second
series wires S1:NC to K3, K3 to K4 and K4 to the coil K2:A1 in WH 0.5.

```python
# easy: a branch across several elements
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU, WH

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
psu = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)
s1 = d.device("S1", "DEMO-CTR-BLOCK-1NO1NC")
s2 = d.device("S2", "DEMO-CTR-BLOCK-1NO1NC")
k2 = d.device("K2", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
k3 = d.device("K3", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
k4 = d.device("K4", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
d.series(dc.plus, s1.nc, s2.no, k2.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
d.series(s1.nc, k3.aux, k4.aux, k2.coil, wire=(WH, 0.5))
```

```python
# efficient: a branch across several elements
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU, WH

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
psu = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)
s1, s2 = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-BLOCK-1NO1NC") for tag in ("S1", "S2"))
k2, k3, k4 = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24") for tag in ("K2", "K3", "K4"))
d.series(dc.plus, s1.nc, s2.no, k2.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
d.series(s1.nc, *(k.aux for k in (k3, k4)), k2.coil, wire=(WH, 0.5))
```

### A changeover in a series

`k1.co_1.no` and `k1.co_1.nc` are the two throws of a changeover, each a series element: line at the
common, load at the throw. The first series that reaches the common wires it once, for both series.
Passing the whole changeover raises: a changeover is two throws, so use `K1.co_1.no` or `K1.co_1.nc`.
Between two fixed terminals a throw is entered and the common leaves: `d.series(x6[2], k1.co_1.no, x7[2])`.
After a supply the common is wired to the supply's poles.

```python
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24"))
k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-RLY-2CO-24")
k2 = d.device("K2", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
k3 = d.device("K3", "DEMO-RLY-2CO-24")
d.series(dc.plus, k1.co_1.no, k2.coil, dc.minus, wire=0.75)
d.series(k1.co_1.nc, k3.coil, dc.minus, wire=0.75)
```

A selector part has its throws on the line side. The series enters it at its throws and draws it
turned.

### Contacts that switch together

`d.poles(k1.co_1, k1.co_2, k1.co_3)` groups one-pole contacts of one device, in pole order, as one
element. It draws as one multi-pole symbol, and each contact keeps its place in the coil's table.
A changeover group gives `.no` and `.nc`. `selector=True` turns its throws to the line, here
selecting supply A or B for M1:

```python
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
xa, xb = d.terminal_strip("XA", "DEMO-TB-2.5"), d.terminal_strip("XB", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
a = d.ac_supply("A", "230", xa[1], xa[2], xa[3], names=("A_L1", "A_L2", "A_L3"))
b = d.ac_supply("B", "230", xb[1], xb[2], xb[3], names=("B_L1", "B_L2", "B_L3"))
qa, qb = d.device("QA", "DEMO-MCB-3P"), d.device("QB", "DEMO-MCB-3P")
k1, m1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-RLY-4CO-24"), d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
q = d.poles(k1.co_1, k1.co_2, k1.co_3, selector=True)
d.series(a, qa.element, q.no, m1, wire=2.5)
d.series(b, qb.element, q.nc, wire=2.5)
```

The pair below feeds a coil from a supply through a bridged run.

```python
# easy: terminal strip and series
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
psu = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
feed = x1.run("coil supply", 3, bridged=True)
k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
k2 = d.device("K2", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
d.series(dc.plus, feed, k1.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
d.series(dc.plus, feed, k2.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
```

```python
# efficient: terminal strip and series
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
psu = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
feed = x1.run("coil supply", 3, bridged=True)


def feed_coil(tag: str) -> None:
    coil = d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24").coil
    d.series(dc.plus, feed, coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))


for tag in ("K1", "K2"):
    feed_coil(tag)
```

### How a series pairs

A series wires each element's load poles to the next element's line poles. The rule:

- Poles pair by conductor mark (`L1`, `L2`, `L3`, `N`) when every end has one, else in order.
- A function is an element when its part names its line side (`side = "line"`, `parts.md`).
- A strip or a cable takes the next free terminal or core, on the side the path enters.
- A path from a supply with `n=` joins N only where an element has a pole for it. A path of three poles
  from a three-phase supply leaves N unwired.
- Connectors pair their pins in pin order when they are a series' two ends.
- A tuple of one device's pins, `(s1.x1[1], s1.x1[4])`, is an element, first or last only; the written order is the pole order. `Fn.pins` lists them.

A refusal starts with one of these texts. Each has one fix.

| refusal starts | fix |
|---|---|
| `<fn> has no pole pair:` | `side` in the part, or `d.detail.wire`; it also fires for over two unmarked pins |
| `<device> has no function of N poles` | pass the function, such as `K1.main`, not the device |
| `<device>: a and b both have poles, say which` | pass the function you mean |
| `N poles into M: name the pins` | pass elements with equal pole counts |
| `conductors L1, L2 into L1, L3: name the pins` | pass elements whose conductor marks agree |
| `<element> has N poles; a path from S takes` | pass the supply's phases, or the phases and N |
| `row <row> value <n> is a bare number, a size` | give the colour and the size as a tuple, such as `("BK", 1.5)` |
| `a pin or a tuple of pins stands only` | put it first or last; else `d.detail.wire` |
| `a changeover is two throws` | pass `K1.co_1.no` or `K1.co_1.nc` |
| `a cable sits between two elements that are not cables` | put a plain element on each side of the cable |
| `<run a> and <run b> both take poles`, `<run> takes poles` | a bridged run in a series, alone or in a parallel, shorts its poles: give each pole its own sized run and take `(x1.run("L1", n, bridged=True)[1], ...)` as a tuple, one terminal per pole |

### Cables

`d.cable("W1", part, length_m=)` adds a cable. Pass it to a series between two elements: each
path takes the next free core, coloured by the cable part, and needs no `wire=`.
`parent=W5` puts the cable in harness `W5`, as on `d.device`.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 4)
w1 = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=5)
d.series(dc.plus, x1, w1, d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24").lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
```

A core with a fixed colour or number is `W1.core(BN, a, b)`: see `detail.md`.
Use `d.pair(x8[1:3], w1, b1.sig)` rather than `d.series` when the ends state no line or load side: core `i` joins pin `i` to pin `i`.

## Wire colours

A colour is an IEC 60757 code imported from `fransys.colours`: `BK`, `BN`, `RD`, `OG`, `YE`, `GN`,
`BU`, `VT`, `GY`, `WH`, `PK`, `GD`, `SR`, `TQ`, and the two-colour `GNYE`. Write `wire=(BU, 0.75)` for
a blue 0.75 mm2 wire.

### Colour by what a wire carries

A design has nine wire rows: `fr.DC_SUPPLY`, `fr.DC_GROUND`, `fr.DC_CONTROL`, `fr.DC_SIGNAL`, `fr.AC_L1`, `fr.AC_L2`,
`fr.AC_L3`, `fr.AC_N` and `fr.AC_CONTROL`. A row's value is a colour, or a colour and a size.
`d.series` picks each wire's row from what it carries.

`fr.design(library, wiring={row: value})` sets rows for the design. `@fr.unit(..., wiring={row: value})`
sets rows for that unit's body. A unit never inherits its parent's rows. With no `wiring=` it draws
the IEC 60204-1 default: AC phases `BK`, `AC_N` `BU`, `AC_CONTROL` `RD`, every DC row `BU`, no sizes.

`d.series(..., wire=)` takes three shapes:

- a size, `wire=0.75`: every wire takes its row's colour at that size.
- a table, `wire={fr.DC_CONTROL: (WH, 0.75)}`: replaces only those rows for this series.
- a spec, `wire=(BU, 0.75)`: every wire gets that colour and size, and the rows are ignored.

A wire whose row has no size and no size on the series is `WIRE_ROW_UNRESOLVED`.

A series that starts on one rail (`dc.plus`, `ac.L1`) is a control path. A wire at the rail's
potential takes the rail's row. A fuse or a contact ends that potential: the wires after it take
`DC_CONTROL` or `AC_CONTROL`. A series that starts on a whole supply (`dc`, `ac`) is a power path:
each pole keeps its conductor's row through every element. On a supply with `n=`, the first
element with poles decides: as many as the phases leaves N unwired, one more takes N. A series that
starts on no rail takes the rows the earlier series gave its net.

A wire with no row when written is resolved at build end (`d.detail` page, "A wire with no row").

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK, RD, WH

d = fr.design("demo_parts", wiring={
    fr.DC_SUPPLY: RD, fr.DC_CONTROL: WH, fr.DC_GROUND: BK,
})
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24"))
s1 = d.device("S1", "DEMO-CTR-BLOCK-1NO1NC")
k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
d.series(dc.plus, s1.no, k1.coil, dc.minus, wire=0.75)  # RD, WH, BK, each 0.75 mm2
```

## Earth pins

`d.earth(*pins)` declares the `PE` net; a wire to the PE terminal builds it. A unit has one `PE` net: each further `d.earth` call in it adds its pins to that net.
Call d.earth before draft(); a later call raises.
Every pin joined by `d.earth` draws the PE symbol, wired or not. A wire to a PE terminal adds its list row. A series through a cable lands its GNYE core on the load's PE port and the strip's next free PE terminal, else open and earthed. A load with no PE port leaves the far end open, the near end on the strip's PE terminal. A single wire to a PE terminal is `d.detail.wire`: see `detail.md`.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import GNYE

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", pe="DEMO-TB-PE-2.5")
pe = x1.run("PE", 2, bridged=True)
m1 = d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
w1 = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=3)
w1.core(GNYE, m1.motor["PE"], pe[1])
d.earth(m1.motor["PE"], pe[1])
```

A PE bar takes its landings. Pass the bar's function where a pin goes: it takes its next free screw
and joins it to the PE net. A bar with every screw taken raises. A bar cut to length from stock writes
no port, so each landing makes a screw. The bar is never drawn; each end on it draws the PE symbol.
A cable core lands on a screw as on any pin; a single wire is `d.detail.wire`: see `detail.md`.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import GNYE

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
pe1 = d.device("PE1", "DEMO-PEBAR-20")
m1 = d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
w1 = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=3)
w2 = d.cable("W2", "DEMO-CBL-2X2X0.75-SP")
w1.core(GNYE, m1.motor["PE"], pe1.pe)  # screw 1
w2.core(5, pe1.pe)  # the one-ended screen, screw 2
```

## AC or DC supply and rails

`d.dc_supply(name, source)` declares a DC supply from the L+ and L- pins of a device; its rails are
`dc.plus` and `dc.minus`, and a series starts or ends on them. With no source device, such as a 24 V
feed on terminals, give the pins and `voltage=`: `d.dc_supply("24VDC", plus=X1[1], minus=X1[2], voltage=24)`.
A source whose part states a nominal voltage takes no `voltage=`. `mid=` adds a middle conductor, as
on a plus and minus 15 V supply.

Without `mid`, `minus` is 0 V and `plus` carries the voltage. With `mid`, `mid` is 0 V, `plus` is
plus the voltage and `minus` is minus the voltage. `names=(plus, minus, mid)` renames the potentials; `ac_supply` takes one name per phase pin, then one for `n`.

`earthing=fr.IT` declares a floating supply; the default is `fr.EARTHED`. Two 0 V rails are two supplies.

`fault_current_a=` is the supply's prospective fault current in amps; `dc_supply` also takes
`fault_time_constant_ms=`. A supply that states one is a source for the breaking-capacity check
(`reading.md`). A `dc_supply` declared from a `source` device refuses both.

A nested unit's declaration of a supply name its container also declares is not a source.

`d.ac_supply(name, voltage, *phases, n=None, names=None)` declares an AC supply on one or three phase pins in
phase order. Its rails are `ac.L1`, plus `ac.L2` and `ac.L3` for three phases. On three phases `voltage` is each phase's RMS to the star point: 230 for a 400 V supply. A pin's side and order
on a rail come from the supply you declare. A rail draws its power symbol only when declared. A fused
branch or a second source of one voltage is not a supply: make it a strip with a `description`, or
wire it point to point. `ac_supply` on a fuse's pins raises "a fused branch is not a supply".
A branch from the common feed is a second series; one looped at the line screws starts at its line pins (`index.md`).

```python
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x0 = d.terminal_strip("X0", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
mains = d.ac_supply("230V", 230, x0[1], n=x0[2])
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", plus=x1[1], minus=x1[2], voltage=24)
```

## Plug a connector

`d.mate(a, b)` plugs connector `a` into connector `b`, each a device with one function
(`units.md` covers a mate across a unit boundary).

## Add a harness

`d.harness("W5")` adds a harness item: see `harnesses.md`.


## Request a PLC channel

`K1.coil.plc(fr.DO, "Pump run")` asks for a digital output named for the signal, and
`.scale("bar", raw=(0, 100), eng=("0", "10"))` scales an analogue one. A series that ends or starts
at a PLC module binds the request to a channel (next section). A request no series wires keeps the
build's own allocation.
`d.rack("U1")` adds the part-less rack the modules sit under with `parent=`; a `d.harness` rack stops with `HARNESS_HOLDS_PLC_MODULE`.

## How channels are numbered

A PLC module passed whole to `d.series` takes its lowest-numbered free channel, as a strip takes
its next free terminal.

| rule | what happens |
|---|---|
| Order | A call takes the lowest free channel when it runs. Calls take channels in the order they run. |
| Direction | A module that ends a path gives an input. A module that starts a path gives an output. A module in the middle of a path raises. |
| Kind | The request on a function of the path, `s1.no.plc(fr.DI, name)`, names the kind. With no request, the module's only kind for that direction. Two kinds and no request raises, naming both kinds and the request that settles it. |
| Fixed | `a1.di_7` is a fixed channel, for one that an existing PLC program or IO list fixes. A fixed channel is taken, and the lowest-free rule skips it. |

Sixteen sensors from a table in IO-list order get channels 1 to 16:

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
a1 = d.device("A1", "DEMO-PLC-DI-16")
io_list = [f"Sensor {n}" for n in range(1, 17)]  # the IO list, in channel order
for number, name in enumerate(io_list, start=1):
    sensor = d.device(f"S{number}", "DEMO-PB-NC")
    sensor.sw.plc(fr.DI, name)
    d.series(dc.plus, sensor.sw, a1, wire=(BU, 0.75))  # S1 takes -A1:1, S2 takes -A1:2, ...
```

To reproduce an existing channel map, write the paths in channel order. Use the fixed form for a
channel that call order cannot reach, such as one after a gap. A program that reads channel 5 after
channel 1 needs `a1.di_5` for the second path. The paths after it continue from channel 2.

```python
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
a1 = d.device("A1", "DEMO-PLC-DI-16")
start, reset, stop = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-PB-NC") for tag in ("S1", "S2", "S3"))
d.series(dc.plus, start.sw, a1, wire=(BU, 0.75))      # channel 1
d.series(dc.plus, reset.sw, a1.di_5, wire=(BU, 0.75))  # fixed: channel 5, after a gap
d.series(dc.plus, stop.sw, a1, wire=(BU, 0.75))       # channel 2: the lowest free one
```

## Title block, revision

`d.project(title=, number=, customer=, ...)` fills the title block and `d.revision(1, date=, text=)`
adds a history line. Both are optional.



---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/detail/index.md -->

# Detail calls

Each call here is for a case no core call writes. Try the core call first (`authoring.md`): a
series pairs poles and takes the next free terminal or core, and layout reads its structure. `d.detail`
is a `fr.Detail` handle, as `d.layout` is a `fr.Layout`.

## When a detail call is right

| call | only for |
|---|---|
| `d.detail.wire(a, b, wire=...)` | two named pins off any path, such as a signal pair; one signal daisy-chained, `d.detail.wire(a, b, c)`; a hop whose printed wire differs from its row |
| `d.detail.star(src, targets, wire=...)` | one point wired to many, one wire each; `d.detail.wire(src, *targets)` chains them instead |
| `X1[3]`, `.inner`, `.outer` | a terminal whose number or side is fixed: a published pinout, or several wires on one terminal |
| `d.pair(a, w1, b)` | a signal pair through a cable, pin for pin, with no line or load side; it is a verb, not a detail |
| `W1.core(BN, a, b)` | a core whose colour or number a termination plan fixes |
| `d.detail.net(name, *pins)` | a named net that no wire joins, such as a bus shown by its label |
| `d.detail.busbar(a, b)`, `d.detail.rail_bond(a, b)` | a rack's internal power jumper; terminals bonded through their mounting rail |

A real circuit that no core call and no row here can write is a gap in Fransys. Report it with its
smallest shape.

## d.detail.wire

`d.detail.wire(a, b, wire=(BU, 0.75), label=, n=)` draws one wire. `wire=` takes the shapes `d.series` takes: a size, a table of rows or a
`(colour, size)`, but not a tuple per pole. A size or a table takes the row of the net. More than two
pins draw a daisy chain, one wire per neighbouring pair. `label="L1"` prints a label on the wire.
`n=2` draws a second wire in parallel between the same two pins. A strip or a run as a pin stands
for its next free terminal, on the inner side.

### One point to many

`d.detail.star(src, targets, wire=...)` draws one wire from `src` to each target in the tuple or list
`targets`, and none between targets. A strip as `src` stands for one terminal, shared by all
targets. `wire=` reads as it does for `d.detail.wire`.

### A wire with no row

A bare number is always a size. A row's value in a table is a colour or a `(colour, size)`, never a
bare number. When `d.series` or `d.detail.wire` cannot give a wire its row as written, the row is
read at build end from the rails its net carries. Only rails of the wire's own unit and the units
below it count. A rail never crosses a unit boundary from its container.

A net that holds a PLC channel's signal takes `DC_SIGNAL`. A pin whose part states `source_row`
(a drive's `U`, `V` and `W`) gives its row. A net with none of these is the error
`WIRE_ROW_UNRESOLVED`, which names the net and the wire; give `wire=(colour, size)` on that series.
A series of only cables, strips and loads needs no `wire=`.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 4)
h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
h2 = d.device("H2", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
d.detail.wire(x1[1], h1[1], wire=(BU, 0.75), label="S1")
d.detail.wire(x1[1], h1[1], wire=(BU, 0.75), n=2)
d.detail.wire(x1[2], h1[2], h2[2], wire=(BU, 0.75))
```

### Equipment others supply

A part-less external strip offers only `.outer`. A field wire on it is a fixed terminal.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x8 = d.terminal_strip("X8", None, 4, external=True)
q8 = d.device("Q8", None, external=True, pins=("L1", "L2", "L3", "N", "PE"))
d.ac_supply("S", 400, q8["L1"], q8["L2"], q8["L3"], n=q8["N"])
d.detail.wire(x8[1].outer, d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")["U"], wire=(BK, 1.5))
```

### Fixed terminals

`X1[3]` takes terminal 3 and `.inner` or `.outer` names its side. A series enters a strip at the
right side by itself. Name a side only when the plan fixes it; `d.series(x1[3].outer, f1.element)` takes it too. A series may also start at a pin: `d.series(k1.coil["A1"], a1.di_1)`.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
with d.function("FEED", "Lamp feed"):
    d.detail.wire(x1[1], h1[1], wire=(BU, 0.75))
d.detail.wire(x1[2].outer, h1[2], wire=(BU, 0.75))
```

### One wire to a PE terminal

A cable's green-yellow core is the core way (`authoring.md`, Earth pins). A single wire is a detail.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import GNYE

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", pe="DEMO-TB-PE-2.5")
pe = x1.run("PE", 2, bridged=True)
m1 = d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
d.detail.wire(m1.motor["PE"], pe[1], wire=(GNYE, 2.5))
d.earth(m1.motor["PE"], pe[1])
```

### A PE bar's screws

A bar's function takes its next free screw (`authoring.md`, Earth pins). One wire to a screw is a detail.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import GNYE

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
pe1 = d.device("PE1", "DEMO-PEBAR-20")
m1 = d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
w2 = d.cable("W2", "DEMO-CBL-2X2X0.75-SP")
d.detail.wire(m1.motor["PE"], pe1.pe, wire=(GNYE, 2.5))  # screw 1
w2.core(5, pe1.pe)  # the one-ended screen, screw 2
```

## d.detail.net, d.detail.busbar, d.detail.rail_bond

`d.detail.net(name, *pins, kind=)` names a net of pins that no wire joins. `kind` is `fr.CONTROL`
(the default), `fr.SIGNAL` or `fr.GENERIC`. It does not make a `PE` or supply net: those have
`d.earth` and the supply calls.

`d.detail.busbar(a, b)` joins two pins by a rack's internal power jumper. `d.detail.rail_bond(a, b)`
joins two terminals bonded through their mounting rail. Neither has a wire-list row, colour or
gauge, and both close the net like a conductor.

```python
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 4)
d.detail.net("BUS", x1[1], x1[2], kind=fr.SIGNAL)
d.detail.busbar(x1[3], x1[4])
d.detail.rail_bond(x1[1], x1[3])
```

## W1.core

`W1.core(BN, a, b)` wires one core between two pins, named by its colour or its number. The core
colours come from the cable part. A green-yellow core goes to a protective-earth pin only.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK, BN, GY

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 8)
pe = d.terminal_strip("X2", "DEMO-TB-PE-2.5", 2)
h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
w1 = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=5)
w1.core(BN, x1[1], h1[1])
w1.core(BK, x1[2], h1[2])
w1.spare(GY, at=x1[7])
w1.spare()
w2 = d.cable("W2", "DEMO-CBL-2X2X0.75-SP", length_m=25)
w2.core(1, x1[3], h1[1])
w2.core(5, pe[1])
w2.spare()
```

A core you leave unused is `w1.spare(GY)`, or `w1.spare()` for every core not wired so far. `at=x1[7]`
parks one on a pin. The cable drawing prints "spare" on its row. A screen (`SH`) earthed at one end
takes one pin: `w2.core(5, pe[1])`. A part with `pairs` in its `[cable_product]` table gets a bracket
and a P1, P2 label over each pair's rows.

`fn.pins` gives a function's pins as a tuple, in the order the connector list prints (`1, 2, 10, A1`).
To land a cable's cores on two connectors pin by pin, loop over it. The pairing rule stays yours.

```python
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
a = d.device("J1", "DEMO-CONN-4P")
b = d.device("J2", "DEMO-CONN-4P")
w3 = d.cable("W3", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=2)
for core, (pin_a, pin_b) in enumerate(zip(a.x1.pins, b.x1.pins, strict=True), start=1):
    w3.core(core, pin_a, pin_b)
```

## Worked example: star-delta winding ends

A star-delta starter wires the six winding ends of a motor. The demo parts have no six-end motor, so
a strip stands for its terminal box: `X2` terminals 1 to 6 are U1, V1, W1, U2, V2, W2. K1 feeds
U1, V1, W1 through a series. K3 joins U1-W2, V1-U2 and W1-V2. K2 shorts U2, V2, W2.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

WIRE = (BK, 2.5)
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x0 = d.terminal_strip("X0", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
ac = d.ac_supply("400V", 230, x0[1], x0[2], x0[3])
k1, k2, k3 = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24") for tag in ("K1", "K2", "K3"))
xm = d.terminal_strip("X2", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 6)
d.series(ac, k1.main, xm, wire=WIRE)
for pole, delta_load in enumerate((6, 4, 5)):  # K3 pole 1 joins U1-W2, 2 V1-U2, 3 W1-V2
    line, load = str(2 * pole + 1), str(2 * pole + 2)
    d.detail.wire(xm[pole + 1], k3.main[line], wire=WIRE)
    d.detail.wire(k3.main[load], xm[delta_load], wire=WIRE)
    d.detail.wire(xm[pole + 4], k2.main[line], wire=WIRE)
d.detail.wire(k2.main["2"], k2.main["4"], k2.main["6"], wire=WIRE)
```

The winding ends stay detail for two reasons. Each end is a fixed terminal, since the motor
plate fixes which end is U2. The star bridge joins three load-side pins that no path pairs.

## Reversing starter

`d.parallel` of two contactors shares the poles in order, so it makes no phase swap. Until an option
for a swap lands, write the reverse contactor's crossing with `d.detail.wire`: K2's line poles 2
and 3 take L3 and L2.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

WIRE = (BK, 2.5)
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x0 = d.terminal_strip("X0", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
ac = d.ac_supply("400V", 230, x0[1], x0[2], x0[3])
k1, k2 = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24") for tag in ("K1", "K2"))
xm = d.terminal_strip("X2", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
d.series(ac, k1.main, xm, wire=WIRE)
for line, crossed in (("1", "1"), ("3", "5"), ("5", "3")):
    d.detail.wire(k1.main[line], k2.main[crossed], wire=WIRE)
for pole, terminal in enumerate((1, 2, 3)):
    d.detail.wire(k2.main[str(2 * pole + 2)], xm[terminal], wire=WIRE)
```

## Flat wiring and fixed terminals on a page

Two drawing effects need a detail call to show, and `drawing.md` states the rules. Point-to-point
`d.detail.wire` hops with no declared supply give layout nets only: one large connected circuit
piles onto a single page and overflows it (`OUT_OF_CONTENT_BOX`). Declare the supply and write each
path as a series, and the same twelve relays spread over pages. A lamp wired from one fixed
terminal of a shared run adds no marker, and neither does a terminal taken in each block.

```python
from pathlib import Path
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


Path("cover.md").write_text("# Cabinet\n", encoding="utf-8")


def built(body):
    @fr.unit(
        "cab", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="First", by="XX",
        title="Cabinet", number="C-1",
    )
    def cabinet(c):
        body(c)
        return Cabinet()

    d = fr.design("demo_parts")
    d.add(cabinet, "U1")
    doc = fr.document(fr.DocumentPreset.CABINET_SCHEMATIC, "cab", cover=Path("cover.md"))
    return fr.build(d, doc)


def relays(c, declare):
    psu = c.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
    dc = c.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output) if declare else None
    for i in range(1, 13):
        with c.function(f"F{i}", f"Relay {i}"):
            k = c.device(f"K{i}", "DEMO-RLY-2CO-24")
        if dc is not None:
            c.series(dc.plus, k.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
        else:
            c.detail.wire(psu.output["+"], k.coil["A1"], wire=(BU, 0.75))
            c.detail.wire(k.coil["A2"], psu.output["-"], wire=(BU, 0.75))


flat = {f.code for f in fr.check(built(lambda c: relays(c, declare=False)))}
declared = {f.code for f in fr.check(built(lambda c: relays(c, declare=True)))}
assert "OUT_OF_CONTENT_BOX" in flat
assert "OUT_OF_CONTENT_BOX" not in declared


def markers(own):
    """Count the link markers of 30 lamp blocks fed from one 24 V run."""

    def body(c):
        psu = c.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
        run = c.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5").run("24V", 40, bridged=True)
        c.detail.wire(psu.output["+"], run[1], wire=(BU, 0.75))
        for i in range(1, 31):
            with c.function(f"F{i}", f"Lamp {i}"):
                lamp = c.device(f"H{i}", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
                c.detail.wire(run[i + 1] if own else run[1], lamp.lamp["1"], wire=(BU, 0.75))
            c.detail.wire(lamp.lamp["2"], psu.output["-"], wire=(BU, 0.75))

    return len(built(body).model.tables["layout.link_marker"])


assert markers(own=True) == markers(own=False)
```

## Layout profile

`d.layout` advises the drawing and connects nothing: `chain`, `keep_together`, `break_before`, `order`,
`symbol`, `draw_in`, `side`, `sheet`, `page_title` and `profile`. Add it last, only where the structure
leaves the drawing a choice. `d.layout.side(u1.bus_in, fr.ABOVE)` puts a unit's interface above its
outline, and `fr.BELOW` below it. An interface with no harness line ignores it.
`d.layout.page_title(x1, "Field terminals")` names the pages drawing a block, function, device or nested unit.

The profile keywords, and the rule that a unit sets its own, are in [`layout-numbers.md`](https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/layout-numbers/index.md#profile-keywords).

`d.layout.chain(r1.lamp, k3.main, f3.element, beside=k1.main)` draws the chain beside the element
`k1.main`, joined by short unmarked horizontals. Wire first: the chain joins the element by each end
net they share, one or two, else `AuthorError` names them.

```python
import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
with d.function("RUN", "Pump run") as run:
    d.device("K1", "DEMO-RLY-2CO-24")
with d.function("LAMPS", "Lamps") as lamps:
    d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
d.layout.order(run, lamps)
d.layout.profile(hide_unused_pins=True)
```

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/harnesses/index.md -->

# Harnesses

This page teaches how to add a harness to a design with `d.harness`, and how its cables and plugs
print. It follows `authoring.md`, which holds the rest of the authoring calls.

## Add a harness

`d.harness("W5")` adds a part-less harness item and returns its handle, which a document can take
as its subject (see `documents.md`). A harness holding a cable needs a tag: `d.harness(name="loom")`
with no tag builds, then fails with `HARNESS_WITHOUT_TAG`. A part-less harness holding exactly one
cable prints that cable as its own designation (`-W5`, its cores `-W5:1`); its plugs stay `-W5-J1`.
With two cables they print `-W5-W1` and `-W5-W2`.
A harness with one cable prints the cable with the harness's designation. The cable's own tag is not printed.

## Wires on a harness

`d.harness("W1")` marks the item as a harness, so plugs and plain wires need no cable. A wire with an
end on a plug of `W1` is a wire of `W1`: `fransys.derive.harness_wires(model, w1_id)` lists its rows.
A wire between plugs of two harnesses is the ERROR `WIRE_ON_TWO_HARNESSES`. A cable beside a wire
prints `-W1-W1`; a cable that is the whole harness prints `-W1`.
A harness of plain wires draws on a harness drawing as one block, with its end boxes and one line per wire, and no cable box.

## Fit a housing on a part's leads

`d.device("J1", "DEMO-HSG-4F", parent=k1, joins={"1": k1.coil["A1"], 2: k1.coil["A2"]})` fits the
housing on the leads of `K1`. Each pair joins a pin of the new device to a pin of `K1`, with no wire
and no cable (a `LEAD` link). The housing prints `-K1-J1`. `joins=` needs a parent device and refuses
a pin twice or a pin of another device with an `AuthorError`.

## Add crimp contacts

`d.device("P1", "DEMO-HSG-4M", parent=w1, contacts="DEMO-CRIMP-M")` fits that contact part in every
used pin of a connector item: a plug, a housing, or any part with a connector function.
A mapping gives mixed contacts: `contacts={"1": "DEMO-CRIMP-M", "2": "DEMO-CRIMP-F"}`.

A used pin is one where a wire or a core lands. The BOM gets one line per contact part. Its count is
the used pins, and its designations are the housings, so one more wire adds one contact.
`contacts=` on a part with no connector function, an unknown pin name or an unknown part raises
`AuthorError`, and the call adds nothing. The contact part is a part file with no function.

## Read a harness line's texts

A cable or harness draws as a harness line when its line carries two or more conductors, cores and single wires together. A cable on a
harness answers for its harness. Read the conductors from `fr.derive.conductors`.

`fransys.derive.harness_line_ends(model, subject)` returns one `HarnessLineEnd` per end of a harness or
cable line. It holds `branch` (the n of `-W13.n`), `plug` or `ports`, and the function `plug` mates.
Cable ends and single-wire ends merge into one order, plugs first by designation. Read the branch
number from it; never number ends yourself.

`fr.derive.line_designation(model, harness, branch)` prints `-W13` between two ends and `-W13.n` on a branch of
three or more. A leaving line prints one stub, `-W3 → +EXT-M1 p2:4A`: the line designation, then each far device with where it is drawn in the same drawing set. A one-conductor cable keeps the per-core form.
A schematic page prints no wire label but a harness line's designation (`-W13`), with one leg per wire
where no plug stands. `line_designation` takes the `unit` of the document that
prints it: on a unit's own document no text names that unit's tag.


---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/units/index.md -->

# Units

A unit is a released, independently built part of a design: a board, a cabinet, a box, anything
built and delivered on its own revision. This page shows how to write one, mark its interface,
record its revisions and nest it in a cabinet. A cabinet is itself a unit: it holds components,
units and wires, and it is never split into places.

`@fr.unit(name, revision=, interface_version=, date=, text=, by=)` turns a Python function into a unit.
The function builds the unit's devices on the design it receives and returns an instance of a
`typing.NamedTuple` class, one field per interface device. `d.add(fn, "U1")` builds the unit into
your design as instance `U1` and returns it, typed. Any other return raises. Every device the function creates belongs to that unit.
`@fr.unit(..., wiring={row: value})` sets the unit's wire rows (authoring.md, Wire colours). With no `wiring=` the unit draws the IEC default, never its parent's rows.

The second argument is the instance's printed tag, bare and with no lowercase letter: `"U3"`,
never `"u3"` or `"-U3"`. It is also the instance's key. A container prints the tag before the
unit's own designation, so a connector `J1` of instance `U3` prints `-U3-J1`. The unit's own document is unchanged.
`None` floats the number: `d.add(fn, None, name="module1")` takes the next free number of the
unit's class code, set with `class_code="U"` on `@fr.unit` (or by the part file's). `name=` is the
identity a released number holds to. A floating add with no `name=` or no class code raises.

`name` is a key, not a designation: write `demo-io-board`, never `-demo-io-board`. A prefix
raises an error. `version=` (default 1), `title=` and `number=` are the unit's own title-block
fields. An empty title or number gives a `TITLE_BLOCK_UNIT_IDENTITY_MISSING` warning on the
unit's own document.

`revision` and `interface_version` are numbers you bump by hand. Revisions count within one
version: a unit's first version runs `1.1`, `1.2`, and so on, and its second version starts again
at `2.1`. `interface_version` is the unit's boundary version.

## The interface

`d.device(tag, part, interface=True)` marks a device as part of the unit's interface: the point a
container may reach into the unit through. Any function may be an interface: a connector, a terminal,
a PLC channel, a coil or a supply output. A cable landing straight on a channel, with no strip
between, is the use. `interface=True` marks every function of the device; `interface=("coil",)`
names some, and the others stay inside the unit.

On a terminal strip `interface=(1, 2)` names terminals by number and `unused=` works the same;
`True` marks every terminal. A run takes `interface=True` or `unused=True` for the whole run. A
container reaches only the boundary terminals, and `d.add(..., unused=("X1",))` covers only those.

`d.device(tag, part, unused=True)` declares an interface device left unconnected on purpose,
so the build does not ask for it to be wired. `unused=True` on a device that is not an
interface marks it as one too. The tuple the function returns names the devices a
container can reach: `io.X1` is the field `X1`. A misspelt field is a type-checker error. A field may hold a nested unit's interface field. That connector, strip, run or terminal becomes this unit's interface too, one level at a time, and prints its full path. The black box a page draws for a nested unit is the unit directly in the page's unit that holds it. A field that holds a strip, a run or a terminal is
typed `fr.TerminalStrip`, `fr.Run` or `fr.Terminal`.
`d.series` and `d.detail.wire` from a container reach the unit strip's free boundary terminals, the PE core the unit's PE run, and never add one.
Carry a strip or a run in the interface when a container wires several terminals in one series, as `io.x5[1:5]`. Separate `fr.Terminal` fields cannot be sliced.

A device with several functions takes the names of the boundary ones: `interface=("x1",),
unused=("x2",)`. `True` takes every function. A name the part lacks raises and lists its
functions; a part class from `fr.parts` rejects it when the type checker runs.

`X1.x1.limits(rating=, operating=)` states the values the unit promises on one boundary
function. Read them from a part with `d.rating(part, fn)` and `d.operating(part, fn)`. It does not
mark the boundary: `interface=True` on the device does. Calling it with no value raises.
`X1[1].limits(rating=, operating=)` does the same for a terminal's boundary, with the same refusals.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Feed(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.TerminalStrip


@fr.unit("demo-supply-strip", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def supply_strip(d):
    x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2, interface=True)
    x1[1].limits(rating=d.rating("DEMO-PSU-24", "input"))
    return Feed(x1)
```

```python
import subprocess
import sys
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr

subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-m", "fransys", "parts-module", "demo_parts", "demo_typed.py"], check=True
)
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import demo_typed as P


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: P.DEMO_CONN_2P


@fr.unit("demo-supply-box", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def box(d: fr.Design) -> Io:
    x1 = d.device("X1", P.DEMO_CONN_2P, interface=True)
    x1.x1.limits(rating=d.rating("DEMO-PSU-24", "input"))
    return Io(x1)
```

Annotate each device field with the generated part class it was built from, as `P.DEMO_CONN_2P`
above. A bare `fr.Device` hides the part's functions from the type checker. A unit may also hand
back a value beside its devices. Annotate that field with its `fr.derive` type, for example
`fr.derive.Operating`, with `| None` where a read may find nothing.

```python
class Supply(NamedTuple):
    X1: P.DEMO_CONN_2P
    rated: fr.derive.Operating | None


@fr.unit("demo-supply-box", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def supply_box(d: fr.Design) -> Supply:
    x1 = d.device("X1", P.DEMO_CONN_2P, interface=True)
    operating = d.operating("DEMO-STRING-864V", "string")
    x1.x1.limits(operating=operating)
    return Supply(x1, operating)
```

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X7: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def board(d):
    return Io(d.device("X7", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


@fr.unit("demo-assembly", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def assembly(d):
    return Io(d.add(board, "U2").X7)  # the board's connector is the assembly's interface too


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
unit = d.add(assembly, "U1")
d.mate(d.device("P1", "DEMO-CONN-2P"), unit.X7)
assert not [f for f in fr.build(d).findings if f.code == "UNIT_BOUNDARY_BYPASSED"]
```

## Leaving one instance open

`unused=True` on `d.device` sits inside the unit, so it marks every instance. A switch's spare ports
are declared once there: `d.device("X2", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True, unused=True)`. To leave the boundary
of one placed instance open, the container names it on `d.add`. `unused=("X1",)` takes every boundary
function of the device in the unit's field `X1`. `unused=("X1.x1",)` takes that one function. A field that holds a tuple of devices takes an index, `"X[0]"` or `"X[0].x1"`. The bare `"X"` takes every element. A
misspelt field raises and lists the fields. A name that is no boundary raises and lists the boundary
functions. A boundary both mated and declared unused still gives `UNUSED_CONTRADICTED`. The check
runs at the unit the `unused=` is on: a function that unit hands up from a nested unit, and wires
across the nested one, is not contradicted.

A field typed `fr.Terminal` names that terminal's one function: `unused=("X1",)`. A field typed
`fr.Run` or `fr.TerminalStrip` names every boundary terminal it holds. `"X1[1].f"` on a terminal
raises. A run or strip with no boundary terminal raises, as a device that is no boundary does.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def board(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit(
    "demo-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    title="Demo cabinet",
    number="DC-1",
)
def cabinet(c):
    io1 = c.add(board, "U1")
    io2 = c.add(board, "U2", unused=("X1",))
    c.mate(c.device("B1", "DEMO-CONN-2P"), io1.X1)
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")
```

The build holds no `BOUNDARY_UNCONNECTED` and no `UNUSED_CONTRADICTED`. U1's `X1` is mated, and U2's
prints `N/A` in its table only.

## Variants and revised copies

A variant is a parameter of your own builders, never a Fransys feature. Fransys has no variant hook,
and nothing patches `fr.Design`. A revised copy of a unit is a factory around `@fr.unit`: a function that
takes the name, the revision and the variant, and returns the decorated unit.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


def board_unit(name: str, revision: int, *, pins: str = "DEMO-CONN-2P") -> fr.UnitDef[Io]:
    @fr.unit(name, revision=revision, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="issue", by="AB")
    def board(d: fr.Design) -> Io:
        return Io(d.device("X1", pins, interface=True))

    return board


first = board_unit("demo-io-board", 1)
revised = board_unit("demo-io-board-r2", 2, pins="DEMO-CONN-4P")
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(first, "U1")
d.add(revised, "U2")
assert len(fr.derive.units(fr.build(d).model)) == 2
```

## Reaching a unit from outside

A container reaches a unit's connector through a plug and `d.mate(plug, io.X1)`. Do not wire
onto the connector's own pins. A direct wire onto a male or female connector of a nested unit
gives the warning `CONNECTOR_WIRED_WITHOUT_MATE`. A screw terminal has no gender and takes the
wire silently. The core lands on the plug's pin (`P1[1]`), because the plug is what the
container's own wiring reaches, and the mate makes plug and connector conduct as one.

A unit built alone, with nothing outside it, leaves its interface unconnected, and
`BOUNDARY_UNCONNECTED` stays silent: an open interface is what the next integrator connects.
The finding fires once the unit sits inside something larger and an interface device is neither
mated nor `unused`.

A nested unit with a harness line at one of its interfaces draws on its parent's page as one
outline, with its columns above and below it. A unit with none keeps its usual frame. Inside stand
