<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/layout-numbers/index.md -->

# Layout numbers

This page lists every keyword of `d.layout.profile` and every number of `d.layout.sheet`: what it does, its house value, its effect on the drawing, and when to change it.
A gap is in grid units `G`; eight `G` make one symbol module. A sheet number is in millimetres, except `module_mm`.

## Sheet numbers

`d.layout.sheet(name, **numbers)` records a sheet format and returns its handle. Pass the handle to `d.layout.profile(sheet=handle)`. A profile with no `sheet` uses the house sheet: A3 landscape, 420 by 297 mm, content box 410 by 267 mm at (5, 5), an 8 by 6 frame, `module_mm` 2.5. A sheet takes all nine numbers and has no defaults. A missing number or an unknown one raises `AuthorError`.

| number | what it is | effect on the drawing | when to change it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `width_mm` | Sheet width. | The size of the printed page. | A different paper size. |
| `height_mm` | Sheet height. | The size of the printed page. | A different paper size. |
| `content_x_mm` | Left edge of the content box, from the sheet's left edge. | Where drawings start; the margin on the left. | A different margin. |
| `content_y_mm` | Top edge of the content box, from the sheet's top edge. | Where drawings start; the margin on top. | A different margin or title block. |
| `content_width_mm` | Width of the content box. | Page capacity: a page holds `content_width_mm * 8 / module_mm` `G` across, rounded down. A wider box fits more columns before a block is split. | A different paper size. |
| `content_height_mm` | Height of the content box. | Page capacity down the page, by the same rule. A taller box fits more rows. | A different paper size. |
| `frame_columns` | Columns of the reference grid printed on the frame. | The content box is divided evenly. Cross references and findings name a position as a column and a row. | Rarely; more columns on a wide sheet. |
| `frame_rows` | Rows of the reference grid. | The same, for rows. | Rarely. |
| `module_mm` | Millimetres of one symbol module. Number or `Decimal`. | The grid pitch. Symbol bodies and gaps scale with it; text sizes and line widths do not, they are fixed in mm. A smaller module fits more on a page; a larger one splits sooner. | The reader's choice of size, not a fix for a crowded page. |

```python
from decimal import Decimal

import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
a4 = d.layout.sheet(
    "A4 landscape",
    width_mm=297,
    height_mm=210,
    content_x_mm=5,
    content_y_mm=5,
    content_width_mm=287,
    content_height_mm=170,
    frame_columns=6,
    frame_rows=4,
    module_mm=Decimal("2.0"),
)
d.layout.profile(sheet=a4)
```

## Profile keywords

`d.layout.profile(...)` sets the layout numbers of the design, or of the unit whose body calls it. At most one per unit. A keyword left out keeps its house value. A value given replaces it whole. A unit with no profile uses the house values, never its parent's. `d.layout.profile` does not draw anything: it advises the layout engine.

| keyword | house value | what it does | effect on the drawing | when to change it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sheet` | the house sheet | The sheet format the pages use, a handle from `d.layout.sheet`. | Paper size, margins and `module_mm`. | A paper size other than A3. |
| `column_gap` | 48 | Clear width between two adjacent columns of blocks. | Wider gaps spread columns and leave room for wires between them. | Wires cramp between columns, or columns waste width. |
| `row_gap` | 32 | The smallest clear height between two blocks stacked in a column. | A column too tall for its page closes its spacing down to this value and no further. | Rarely; lower it to fit a tall column. |
| `row_spacing` | 88 | The clear height a block keeps below the one above it, when the page has room. | Looser spacing reads easier; it falls back toward `row_gap` on a full page. | A sparse page that wastes height, or a crowded one. |
| `route_margin` | 64 | How far outside the box spanned by a wire's two ends the router may look first. | A larger margin finds a detour round a block; a smaller one keeps wires short. | A wire takes a long way round, or cannot find a way. |
| `text_height_mm` | 1.8 | The smallest text on every page kind, a capital height in mm (ISO 3098); a larger role keeps its own size or this one, whichever is larger. | Sets text size, and with it the room texts take: font size over one `G`, rounded up. | A style choice only. See below. |
| `min_text_height_mm` | 1.8 | The smallest capital height in mm the text may print at. | Changes no drawing. A profile printing under the floor gets one `TEXT_TOO_SMALL` warning, and nothing is shrunk or grown. | The recommended floor is the house 1.8. Lower it only when the small text is intended. Otherwise raise `text_height_mm`. |
| `marker_padding` | 2 | Clear space between a link marker's text and its outline, on every edge. | Larger padding makes markers and their boxes bigger. | Markers look cramped. |
| `route_turn_penalty` | 4 | The cost of one bend in a wire. | A higher cost makes wires straighter and longer. | Wires zigzag. |
| `route_crossing_penalty` | 16 | The cost of one wire crossing another. | A higher cost avoids crossings at the price of longer wires. | Too many crossings. |
| `hide_unused_pins` | `False` | Hide a box-drawn pin with no conductor, and a function with none, on drawings only. | Drawings are shorter; every list still shows every pin. A box in a chain draws only its wired pins (LONG-CHAIN D2). | An interface with many unused pins. |
| `actuator_each_contact` | `True` | Draw the operated symbol on every contact of a manually operated device, with no reference and no contact list. | `False` draws the actuator once at the lead contact, with the contact list under it. | A design that wants one push button per device. The choice is per unit: set it in each unit's profile, or in a shared helper every unit calls, to set it once. |
| `band_ranks` | supply 0, `terminal.first` 0, protection 1, switch and contacts 2, sensor 3, coil, load, actuator and `terminal` 4, `terminal.last` 5 | A map of function kind to the horizontal band it sits in, top first. `terminal.first` and `terminal.last` sit beside `terminal`. | Moves kinds up or down the column. The map replaces the house map whole: restate every kind you want ranked. | A circuit reads better with another top-to-bottom order. |
| `group_ranks` | empty | A map of an aspect group's label to its page rank. | Orders the groups of pages. A group with no rank sorts last. | You want the pages in your own order. |

## Grid pitch and printed sizes

`module_mm` sets the grid pitch, not the printed size of text or lines, which are fixed in mm. It is the reader's choice of size, never a fix for a crowded page. Split the content into function blocks (`drawing.md`). A well-formed design that still overflows is a Fransys defect: send the smallest model.
`text_height_mm` sets the smallest text on every page, as a capital height in mm. Never use it to make a page fit: a page that is too full needs less on the page, split into function blocks.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/reading-rows/index.md -->

# Reading: rows, columns and printed texts

This page covers `fr.derive`, the facade's read-only layer. It holds the column orders and labels of the list outputs and the row types they are built from. It also holds the row functions, and the texts and order keys every list shares. Use these to read a model yourself and get the same numbers, text and order the outputs print.

## Column and label constants

Each constant is a tuple or a dict of field names. The list outputs read them in order, so a column appears where its name appears here.

- `BOM_COLUMNS` is `('mpn', 'revision', 'manufacturer', 'description', 'count', 'designations')`. It orders the columns of the bill of materials list.
- `CABLE_LIST_COLUMNS` is `('designation', 'mpn', 'description', 'core_count', 'gauge_mm2', 'length_mm', 'from_label', 'to_label', 'pairs')`. It orders the columns of the cable list. The two `*_label` columns are the far-end texts of the cable.
- `CORE_LIST_COLUMNS` is `('cable', 'core', 'colour', 'pair', 'end_a', 'end_b', 'note')`. It orders the columns of the core list. `pair` is the core's pair word, `note` is `spare` for a spare core.
- `DESIGNATION_COLUMNS` is `('designation', 'reference', 'description')`. It orders the columns of the designation list: the printed designation, the full reference and the description.
- `CONNECTOR_COLUMNS` is `('designation', 'style', 'pincount', 'gender', 'mate_designation')`. It orders the connector part of the connector list. Each pin line repeats these fields.
- `PIN_COLUMNS` is `('marking', 'net', 'mate_port_designation', 'ends')`. It orders the pin part of the connector list, after `CONNECTOR_COLUMNS`. One line per pin.
- `CONNECTOR_LABELS` is `{'marking': 'Pin', 'mate_port_designation': 'Mate'}`. It gives the headings of those two columns in the connector table of a PDF.
- `PLC_COLUMNS` is `('pin', 'channel_name', 'signal', 'signal_name', 'wired_to')`. It orders the PLC list, which has one row per pin. The field device is not printed in this list, although the row carries it.
- `TERMINAL_COLUMNS` is `('designation', 'group', 'index', 'internal_ends', 'external_ends', 'jumper_group')`. It orders the terminal list of a strip.
- `TERMINAL_LABELS` is `{'internal_ends': 'Side A', 'external_ends': 'Side B'}`. It gives the headings of the two far-end columns of a terminal list. The CSV file writes them in snake case, as `side_a` and `side_b`.
- `WIRE_COLUMNS` is `('from_', 'to', 'colour', 'cross_section_mm2', 'label')`. It orders the wire list.
- `WIRE_LABELS` is `{'from_': 'from'}`. It changes only the heading of the `from_` column, which the field name cannot hold, so the wire list prints `from`.
- `CELL_SEPARATOR` is `'; '`. It joins the parts of one list cell that holds more than one value, such as several far ends of a terminal. Empty parts are left out.

## Row types

Every row is a frozen record. A row is the one shape an output reads, so the layout and the renderers never look up the model for these facts.

- `CableRow` is one core of one cable, both ends. Fields: `cable`, `cable_designation`, `index`, `colour`, `conductor`, `end_a`, `end_a_designation`, `end_b`, `end_b_designation`. The ends are ports; the designations are their printed text.
- `ChannelScaling` is the scaling of a field device, projected so a formatter never looks it up. Fields: `unit`, `raw_min`, `raw_max` (integers), and `eng_min`, `eng_max` (decimals).
- `ConnectorPin` is one pin of a board connector. Fields: `port`, `marking`, `net`, `mate_port`, `mate_port_designation`, `ends`. The `marking` is the port's name. The `net` is the declared net that lists the port, or `None` when none does. The mate's pin is the port of the same name on the mated function. The `ends` are the far ends of every conductor on the pin or on its mate, as a terminal row prints them; empty when there is none.
- `ConnectorRow` is one connector of a board, as `connector_rows` lists it. Fields: `connector`, `designation`, `style`, `pincount`, `gender`, `mate`, `mate_designation`, `pins`. The `gender` is `None` when the part file states none. The `mate` is `None` when the connector is unmated. The `pins` is a tuple of `ConnectorPin`.
- `DesignationRow` is one line of the designation list. Fields: `item`, `designation`, `reference`, `description`. The `designation` is the printed designation, and `reference` is the reference designation.
- `HarnessCore` is one core of a harness cable, with the label its wire carries. Fields: `conductor`, `index`, `colour`, `label`, `end_a`, `end_a_designation`, `end_b`, `end_b_designation`. The `label` is `None` when the wire has none. Every core of one cable runs from the same physical end to the same other end.
- `HarnessEnd` is one item that a core lands on: a connector housing, a plain device, or a strip of terminals. Fields: `item`, `designation`, `connector`, `style`, `pincount`, `gender`, `mpn`, `pins`. The `designation` is the item's product designation for every end. The connector fields are `None` for a plain device or a strip. When a core lands on a terminal with a parent, `item` is the strip, and `pins` holds one `HarnessPin` per landed terminal.
- `HarnessPin` is one port of a harness end that a core lands on. Fields: `port`, `marking`. The `marking` is the port's own name. For a terminal in a strip it is the bare `group:index` text, such as `L1:1`, without the strip's designation, because the end already prints the strip.
- `PlcChannelRow` is one pin of a PLC channel. Fields: `channel`, `port`, `pin`, `channel_name`, `signal`, `wired_to`, `field_device`, `field_device_designation`, `signal_name`. The `pin` is the pin's printed designation (`-A2:5`) and `channel_name` the channel's own number. The `wired_to` joins the far ends of that pin's conductors with `CELL_SEPARATOR`, or is `None` when nothing is printed. The three field fields are `None` for a channel with no bound device.
- `PlcRackChannel` is one channel of a rack module, bound or spare. Fields: `channel`, `number`, `signal`, `field_device`, `field_device_designation`, `signal_name`, `scaling`. The field fields are `None` for a spare channel. The `scaling` is `None` when the bound device has no scaling facet.
- `PlcRackModule` is one PLC module of a rack, with its channels in order. Modules go by `position`, else by their own tag. Channels with one number go by the function names in the part file, in natural order. A block tag never changes the order of racks, modules or channels (model-0259). Fields: `module`, `designation`, `mpn`, `description`, `position`, `channels`. The `mpn` and `description` come from the part. The `position` is `None` when the author never gave one.
- `PlcTable` is one table of the PLC list: the channels of one controller or module. Fields: `item`, `designation` and `rows`. `item` carries the channels, `designation` is its printed designation and the table's heading, and `rows` are its `PlcChannelRow`s in list order, never empty.
- `BoardNetlist` is a board's parts, footprints and nets. Fields: `board`, `board_designation`, `parts`, `nets` and `without_footprint`. `without_footprint` lists the board's parts whose part carries no footprint; a netlist cannot place them, so `parts` omits them. An accessory prints its holder's designation, so it is never listed.
- `NetlistPart` is one placed part of a `BoardNetlist`. Fields: `item`, `designation` (relative to the board), `mpn`, `footprint_library`, `footprint_name` and `installed`. `installed` is the item's own flag: a part not installed stays listed, and the output decides what to do with it.
- `NetlistNet` is one net of a `BoardNetlist`. Fields: `name` and `pins`, the ports it joins.
- `TerminalRow` is one terminal of a strip's connection list. Fields: `terminal`, `designation`, `group`, `index`, `internal`, `external`, `internal_ends`, `external_ends`, `jumper_group`. An unused terminal has empty `internal` and `external` tuples. Bridged terminals share one `jumper_group` number. The `internal_ends[i]` is the far end of `internal[i]`, and the same for `external`.

## Row functions

Each function takes a frozen model and returns rows. None of them writes a file or reads a clock. Most raise a schema error when a named item, function or unit is not in the model, or when an item has no designation. `boards` takes no such check.

- `boards` returns the ids of every item whose part carries a board facet. It sorts them by natural designation, then by id. The export enumeration and the PDF document contents use this same function, so they agree on what a board is.
- `cable_rows` returns one `CableRow` per core of a cable. Cores sort by their index, then by conductor id. Its `unit` keyword keeps the cores drawn by one unit's document.
- `designation_list` returns one `DesignationRow` per item, terminals included, sorted by designation, then id. An accessory that takes its parent's designation has no row. Its `unit` keyword keeps the rows of one unit only; the unit's sole root has no row.
- `board_netlist` takes a model and a board item. It returns the `BoardNetlist` of that board. Its parts are the footprinted descendants of the board. Its nets join the board's internal conductors and its declared nets, never `Mate`s. It raises a schema error when the board is not an item of the model, or when it or a listed item has no designation. Use it to check a board's connectivity yourself; the KiCad export builds the same netlist.
- `plc_channel_rows` returns one `PlcChannelRow` per pin of each PLC channel function, in list order: channels as the PLC list orders them, the pins of a channel by name. Its `unit` keyword keeps one unit's channels. Its `context` keyword sets the location the list prints for, and it has no effect once `unit` is given.
- `plc_tables` returns the rows of `plc_channel_rows`, grouped into one `PlcTable` per carrying item, in the same order. A controller's own channels form its table, the modules' tables follow in rack order, and items in no rack come last, one table each. An item with no channel has no table. Its `unit` and `context` keywords are those of `plc_channel_rows`. Use it when you print one table per controller or module, as the PLC list does.
- `signal_word` returns the word a printed list uses for a `SignalType`: `DI`, `DO`, `AI (V)`, `AI (mA)`, `AO (V)`, `AO (mA)`, `RTD` or `DO (relay)`. The CSV keeps the enum value.
- `plc_list_rows` takes `PlcChannelRow`s and returns one `PLC_COLUMNS` tuple per row for a printed list. The signal is its `signal_word`. A channel with no device and no wire prints `spare` as its signal name.
- `terminal_rows` returns one `TerminalRow` per terminal of a strip. Terminals sort by the natural key of their group, then by index, then by id. A far end outside the given `context` prints with its location path in front, such as `+EXT-M1:U1`. A far end inside it prints short, such as `-B12:2/T1`.

- `open_core_rows(model, cable, *, unit=None)` returns one `OpenCoreRow` per open core of `cable`, by core number. An open core is a spare or a screen earthed at one end. A row holds the core's `index`, `colour`, the port it lands on (`at`, `at_designation`; `None` and `""` for none) and `spare`, false for an `SH` screen. `HarnessCable.open_cores` holds the same rows.
- `core_list_rows(model, *, unit=None)` returns one `CoreListRow` per core of every cable `cable_list_rows` lists. The order is the cable list's, then core number. The wired cores and the open ones are in it, and the ends print as the cable drawing prints them. A spare parked on a pin has it as `end_a`. `pair` is `P1` or `screen P1`, `""` outside a pair, and `note` is `spare` for a spare core. `CORE_LIST_COLUMNS` names the fields, in print order. `cores.csv` is this list.
- `contents_rows(cables)` reshapes a tuple of `HarnessCable`s into one `ContentsRow` per cable. The tuple comes from `harness_cables`, `top_level_cables` or `unit_cables`. The row keeps the cable's product facts and adds `ends`. That is every end's designation, in the cable's own order, joined by an en dash, and a blank end drops its dash. `CONTENTS_COLUMNS` names its columns, in print order.

## Printed texts and order keys

These functions give the one text and the one order that each list uses. A list that prints a label or sorts a column calls them rather than building its own.

- `cable_title` returns the cable's printed title. It is its designation, then a space and its MPN when the cable has one. Without an MPN it is the designation alone.
- `function_designation` renders a function as its item's designation, a colon and the function's name, such as `JB1:J1`. Its `unit` keyword sets whether the text is written for one unit's document or for the whole model.
- `item_description` returns the text a list shows for an item. It is the item's own description, else its part's description, else an empty string. The part's text is never copied onto the item.
- `release_order` returns the order key of a unit release or a history entry, from a version and a revision as two integers. The key is a pair of integers, so revision 10 sorts after revision 9. Compare releases with this key, never with printed text, because the text `"1.10"` sorts before `"1.9"`.
- `sideless_pins` gives the pins of two series ends that have no line side, each in pin order, as `SidelessPins(first, second, problem)`. It takes a label and a tuple of port templates for each end. The order is the marking by value, and the pin's name when it prints none. `problem` is the message that says why the ends cannot pair, or `None`. They cannot pair with a different number of pins, or the same names in another order. A series between two connectors pairs their pins with it.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/reading-records/index.md -->

# Reading: records, lookups and ratings

This page covers the records that describe a model's structure, the lookups that find them,
and the ratings and currents that say what a circuit may carry. Each record type has a
table function that returns every record of that type, keyed by id. Every name here is
reached as `fr.derive.NAME`.

## Records

- `Aspect` is one of the three IEC 81346 views of the same objects: `FUNCTION`, `PRODUCT` and `LOCATION`.
- `AspectNode` is a node in one aspect tree. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `aspect`, `parent` (an `AspectNode` id, or `None` at the root), `label`, `description` and `ext`. A `LOCATION` node with label `C1` is the place `+C1`. The table is `aspect_nodes`.
- `Placement` puts one item at one aspect node. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `item`, `node` and `ext`. An item has at most one placement per aspect, so one item can have a product placement and a location placement. The table is `placements`.
- `Boundary` marks a function as part of a unit's interface. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `unit`, `function`, `name` and `ext`. `name` is the field name the unit gave the function, or `None`. One function can be the boundary of several units. The table is `boundaries`.
- `Port` is a connection point on a function. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `function`, `template`, `name`, `role`, `marking` and `ext`. `template` is `None` for a port without a part template. The `marking` field is the pin text printed on the drawing: `None` prints the port's name, an empty string prints nothing, and any other string prints as given.
- `PortRole` says what a port is for. Its members are `GENERIC`, `INTERNAL`, `EXTERNAL`, `PE`, `COMMON`, `BREAK` and `MAKE`. A terminal's two ports are `INTERNAL` (panel side) and `EXTERNAL` (field cable side). A contact's ports are `COMMON`, `BREAK` (closed at rest) or `MAKE` (closed when operated).
- `Conductor` is a physical connection with exactly two ends. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `a`, `b`, `kind`, `carrier` (the item that carries it, or `None`) and `ext`. `a` and `b` are stored in id order, so they do not say a direction. The table is `conductors`.
- `ConductorKind` says what realises a conductor. Its members are `WIRE`, `CORE`, `JUMPER`, `BUSBAR`, `MOUNT`, `RAIL` and `LEAD`. `MOUNT`, `BUSBAR`, `RAIL` and `LEAD` are links: they close a net and are never wires.
- `PhysicalNet` is one net found from real connectivity: a maximal set of ports joined by conductors. Its only field is `ports`, sorted by id. It differs from a declared net, which is the intent the author wrote. Two closures over the same wiring compare equal.
- `NetClass` says what kind of potential or signal a `Net` carries. Its members are `POWER`, `CONTROL`, `SIGNAL`, `PE` and `GENERIC`. A 24 V supply rail is `POWER`; a 4-20 mA transmitter loop is `SIGNAL`. Read it as `net.net_class` on a row of `fr.derive.nets`.

## Lookups

- `aspect_nodes(model)` returns every `AspectNode`, keyed by id. It is the model's own table, not a copy, and it is empty when the model has none.
- `placements(model)` returns every `Placement`, keyed by id, in the same way.
- `boundaries(model)` returns every `Boundary`, keyed by id, in the same way.
- `conductors(model)` returns every `Conductor`, keyed by id, in the same way.
- `item_location(model, item)` returns the id of the `LOCATION` node the item is placed at. It uses the item's own placement, or the nearest placed ancestor's. It returns `None` when there is none. It raises `SchemaError` when `item` is not an item of the model.
- `items_at(model, node)` returns the ids of every item at `node` or at any node below it, once each and sorted by id. An item counts by its own placement, or by its nearest placed ancestor's. It raises `SchemaError` when `node` is not an aspect node of the model.
- `effective_placement(model, item, aspect)` returns the id of the `AspectNode` where `item` sits in `aspect`: its own placement, else its nearest placed ancestor's, else `None`. It walks `Item.parent` and stops on a cycle. A tie in one aspect resolves to the smallest placement id. It raises `SchemaError` when `item` is not an item of the model. Use it when you need one aspect's node; `item_location` is its `LOCATION` case.
- `subtree` takes a model and a node. It returns the ids of every descendant of `node`, following `parent`, with `node` itself left out. The result is sorted by id. It follows `parent` in any aspect and stops on a cycle. It raises `SchemaError` when `node` is not an aspect node.
- `net_of` takes a model and a port. It returns the `PhysicalNet` that contains the port. It returns `None` when the port is not a port of the model.
- `revision_history` takes a model and an optional release. It returns the `Revision` records of a release, in date order, then by version and revision as numbers, so revision 2 comes before revision 10. With `release=None` it returns the project's own history. It raises `SchemaError` when `release` is not `None` and is not a release of the model.

Use `item_location` when a list needs an item's place and the place may be inherited. Use `items_at` when you need everything in a cabinet or on a board, including the items under it.

## Ratings and currents

- `Rating` says what a function or a part is rated for. Its fields are `voltage_ac_v`, `voltage_dc_v`, `current_ac_a`, `current_dc_a`, `min_breaking_current_a`, `power_loss_w`, `breaking_ac` and `breaking_dc`. A field is `None` when the datasheet gives no value. AC voltages are RMS, and DC voltages are the highest permissible potential. Currents are continuous ratings, except `min_breaking_current_a`, which is the lowest current a partial-range fuse breaks. The model checks the types only; comparing a rating with the plant is a check's job.
- `CurrentPosition` is one rated current path. Its fields are `functions` (sorted), `bounds` and `ports`. `bounds` holds at most one `CurrentBound` per current kind, AC before DC. `ports` are the two end ports of the path, and they tell apart paths that pass through the same functions, one per pole.
- `CurrentChain` is a block of the current graph. Its only field is `positions`, in the order that the chain lists them. The graph treats every switched link as closed. A position that exists only in some switch state is a chain on its own.
- `LimitRole` says what set a bound. Its members are `SOURCE`, a source's continuous limit, and `PROTECTION`, a full-range protective device.
- `port_potential_current` takes a model and a port. It returns the current kind, `AC` or `DC`, of the supply behind the port's potential. It returns `None` when the port has no potential rank, and it always returns `None` for protective earth, which belongs to no supply.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/keywords/index.md -->

# Keywords and handles

This page lists the public names of the facade's handles and signal types, then the keyword
arguments of the record constructors. The keywords of the `d.*` calls are in `keywords-design.md`,
those of the handle methods and layout hints in `keywords-handles.md`, those of the `fr.*` functions in `keywords-output.md`.

## Signal types and short names

A signal type says what kind of PLC channel or field signal a function asks for. The facade
gives the common ones short names. `fr.DI`, `fr.DO`, `fr.AI` and `fr.AO` are all members of
`fr.SignalType`, and each is passed as the `signal` of `plc`.

- `DI`: a digital input, `SignalType.DI`.
- `DO`: a digital output, `SignalType.DO`. `DO` belongs with `DI`, `AI` and `AO` as one of the four short names.
- `AI`: an analog input, the 4-20 mA current loop, `SignalType.AI_CURRENT`. Analog voltage inputs have no short name.
- `AO`: an analog output, the 4-20 mA current loop, `SignalType.AO_CURRENT`. Analog voltage outputs have no short name.

The short names cover only the current loops and the
two digital kinds. Use the full member, `fr.SignalType.<NAME>`, for the rest:

- `fr.SignalType.AI_VOLTAGE` and `fr.SignalType.AO_VOLTAGE`: analog voltage inputs and outputs.
- `fr.SignalType.RTD`: a resistance temperature detector, such as a Pt100.
- `fr.SignalType.RELAY`: a relay signal.

```python
import fransys as fr

assert fr.DI is fr.SignalType.DI
assert fr.AI is fr.SignalType.AI_CURRENT
rtd = fr.SignalType.RTD  # no short name; pass it as the `signal` of `plc`
```

## Handle types

Handles are the objects a design returns and the reader holds. A consumer does not build them.

- `Device`: one device, such as `Q1`. It reaches a function by name (`Q1.coil`) and a pin by brackets (`Q1[2]`). An unknown function or pin raises and lists the candidates. `Q1.tag` is the tag the call gave, or `None`.
- `Fn`: one function of a device, such as `K1.coil`. It reaches a pin by brackets (`Q1.main[2]`) or by name (`K1.coil.A1`). An unknown pin raises and lists the pins it has. `Fn.plc` requests a PLC channel.
- `Pin`: one port of one `Fn`. It has an `id`, an authoring `key`, a `name` that brackets match, and a `role`, such as `INTERNAL` or `EXTERNAL`.
- `Run`: a run of terminals on a strip, from `x1.run(...)`. It reaches a terminal by brackets (`run[1]`).
- `Cable`: one cable from `d.cable`. `w1.core(BN, a, b)` wires a core.
- `AcSupply`: what `d.ac_supply` returns. It holds the rails `L1`, `L2`, `L3` and `N` when it was given one.
- `DcSupply`: what `d.dc_supply` returns. It holds the rails `plus`, `minus` and `mid`.
- `SupplyRail`: one rail of a supply, such as `supply.L1` or `supply.plus`.
- `UnitDef`: what `@fr.unit` returns, the release of one unit. `d.add(definition, "U1")` builds it; a function that takes build arguments returns one.
- `Throw`: one throw of a changeover, `k1.co.no` or `k1.co.nc`. It stands in a `d.series` call as an element. A consumer does not build one (its `fns` are the changeover functions). A generated parts module declares it on every changeover function.
- `TypedDevice`: the base a generated parts module subclasses once for each part. Its `mpn` is its whole contract. It adds no behaviour: the subclass only declares functions and pins.
- `TypedFn`: the base a generated parts module subclasses for one function of one part. It adds no behaviour. Its subclass declares pins for the type checker.
- `BuildResult`: the result of `fr.build`. It holds `model`, the frozen and laid-out `Model`, and `findings`, every finding collected while building it.

## Type checking

A script written in this guide's spellings type-checks with no `ty: ignore` and no `Any`. Your ty settings need nothing.

- For full checking, generate a parts module (`fr.parts_module`, parts.md) and pass its classes to `d.device`. Each function and pin is a typed attribute, brackets take only the part's pin names, and a misspelt name is a type error.
- A device made from an MPN string is checked only at run time: a call on it checks nothing. Annotate it `fr.Device` to check the calls on it.
- On a `fr.Device`, a device-level pin by attribute (`q1.A1`) types as `fr.Fn` and is a ty error where a pin is needed. Write `q1["A1"]`; both run.
- Every handle in "Handle types" has a name on `fr`, so `fr.Device`, `fr.AcSupply` or `fr.UnitDef[Io]` annotates a parameter or a return.
- A function of a device is a `fr.Fn`: `k1.coil` and `q1.main` type as `fr.Fn`. A pin by brackets is a `fr.Pin`: `k1.coil["A2"]`, `q1["2"]` and `k1.coil.A1`. `k1.co.no` and `k1.co.nc` are changeover throws (`fr.Throw`); a generated changeover function declares both.
- A pin chosen by an `int` loop variable is a ty error against a typed part's pin names: loop over `fn.pins`. A computed name, `f"CH {n}"`, is a ty error too.
- A wrong function or pin name is a run-time error. It raises and lists the names the part has. A pin named `+` or `-` is the attribute `_plus` or `_minus`.
- A unit with build arguments is a factory that returns `fr.UnitDef` (units.md, "Variants and revised copies").

## Severity

`Severity` says how much a `Finding` blocks a downstream output. The facade alone decides which
severities block which outputs.

- `ERROR`: blocks every export. `write` raises and writes nothing while any error finding remains. There is no escape hatch.
- `WARNING`: worth a look. It blocks nothing under the facade's policy.
- `INFO`: worth noting. It blocks nothing under the facade's policy.

## Model and Finding

The facade builds these records. A consumer reads them and does not construct them. `freeze`
builds a `Model`, and the domain validators and the facade build the `Finding` values.

### Model

`Model` is the immutable, validated result of `freeze`. Everything reachable from it is deeply immutable, and `freeze` checks that.

- `schema_version`: the model schema number. `freeze` stamps the number this build knows. Reading data with a number this build does not know raises an error.
- `aliases`: a map from a retired id to the id that replaces it. `freeze` rewrites every reference to a retired id into one to its replacement. `Draft.alias` fills it.
- `origins`: a map from an id to its `Origin`, the file, line and note where the record was authored. It sits outside the tables. Moving a line does not change the digest.
- `digests`: one digest for each registered namespace, such as `core`, `facet` or `layout`. A change to `layout` records leaves the `core` and `facet` digests alone.
- `digest`: one digest that combines the `digests`. A generated parts module records it as its library digest. `fr.design` refuses a stale module, so a library change must be regenerated before use.
- `Model.origin_of` and `Model.key_of` read `origins` and the tables. See `target` below.

### Finding

`Finding` is one reported engineering problem. Every domain validator emits this one shape. All four fields are required keyword arguments.

- `code`: a stable `UPPER_SNAKE` string, such as `NET_UNREALISED`. The module that emits it lists it. The reader sees it in the findings list. The order is error, warning, then info, and inside each band by `code`, then `subjects`, then `message`.
- `severity`: a `Severity`. Only `ERROR` stops an export. See the Severity section above.
- `subjects`: the ids the finding is about. They are stored once each, in id order, so the order a validator found them in does not matter.
- `message`: the text a reader sees. For a `write` finding the facade's `describe` turns it into printed text first. A `release` finding prints its message as written.

## Draft calls

A `Draft` collects records from input files before `freeze`. Inputs call these methods. A consumer
rarely does.

- `origin` on `Draft.add` and `Draft.extend`: the `Origin` the records are attributed to. It is required, with no default. An identical record already present keeps the smaller origin by `(file, line, note)`, so call order does not matter. A different record under the same id raises a merge conflict. `extend` is not atomic: a conflict leaves the records before it in place.
- `old` on `Draft.alias`: the id that has been retired. The `new` argument is its replacement. It raises when `old` is `new`, the two are of different kinds, or `old` is already retired in favour of another id. The input decoder and the merge both call it.
- `target` on `Draft.key_of`, `Draft.origin_of` and `Draft.record_of`: the id to look up. `key_of` returns the record's authoring key, `origin_of` returns its `Origin`, and `record_of` returns the record itself. Each returns `None` when nothing is held. `record_of` does not follow an alias.
- `target` on `Model.key_of` and `Model.origin_of`: the same lookup on a frozen `Model`. `key_of` returns `None` when no record holds the id. `origin_of` returns the `Origin` or `None`. The `describe` function asks it where an id was written.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/keywords-design/index.md -->

# Keywords of the d calls

This page has one table for each `d.*` and `d.detail.*` call: each named keyword, its default, its effect and an example fragment.
A call that takes only `*args` has no table, and one sentence says what it takes.

`place=` is the same on every call that takes it: the `place=` table in `authoring.md` says what it changes.
The `fr.*` functions are in `keywords-output.md`, the handle methods and layout hints in `keywords-handles.md`.

## `d.device`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tag` | required | The printed tag, bare and with no lowercase letter. `None` numbers the device from its class code and needs `name=`. | `d.device("Q1", P.Q)` |
| `part` | required | A part class or an MPN string. `None` makes an `external=True` box of `pins=`, with a tag and no BOM line. | `d.device("Q1", "DEMO-MCB-3P")` |
| `pins` | `None` | Names the pins of a part-less box (`part=None`). Ignored for a real part. | `d.device("A1", None, pins=("1", "2"), external=True)` |
| `place` | `...` | Where the device stands. See the `place=` table in `authoring.md`. | `d.device("Q1", P.Q, place="HOLD")` |
| `parent` | `None` | The device, strip or cable that holds this one. An accessory prints its holder's designation and uses no number. | `d.device("J1", P.HSG, parent=k1)` |
| `name` | `None` | The key a released number holds to. A floating device, with `tag=None`, raises without it. | `d.device(None, P.Q, name="main-breaker")` |
| `interface` | `False` | Marks the device's functions as the unit's boundary: `True` marks all, a tuple of function names marks those. | `d.device("X1", P.CONN, interface=True)` |
| `unused` | `False` | Marks functions as unused, so no unused-pin finding is raised for them: `True` marks all, a tuple marks those. | `d.device("X1", P.CONN, unused=("x2",))` |
| `mounted_on` | `None` | Mounts the device on a carrier device or function, as a contactor on a protective switch. The carrier's load pins join this device's line pins pole by pole. | `d.device("K1", P.CTR, mounted_on=q1)` |
| `joins` | `None` | Maps the housing's pins to the parent's pins. A housing fitted on a parent's own leads joins them with no wire. Needs `parent=` to be a device. | `d.device("J1", P.HSG, parent=k1, joins={1: k1.coil["A1"]})` |
| `description` | `''` | Text for the designation list in place of the part's description. Empty falls back to the part's. | `d.device("Q1", P.Q, description="Pump breaker")` |
| `position` | `None` | The physical order within the parent, such as the slot of a PLC module or a place on a rail. It orders the rack and the lists. | `d.device("A2", P.DI8, parent=rack, position=2)` |
| `installed` | `True` | `False` keeps the device in drawings and reservations but drops it from the BOM. | `d.device("Q9", P.Q, installed=False)` |
| `external` | `False` | `True` marks the device as supplied by others: no BOM line, and every drawing marks it dashed "(by others)". | `d.device("M1", P.MOTOR, external=True)` |
| `contacts` | `None` | Fits a contact part in every pin of a housing, or a mapping of pin name to part for mixed contacts. | `d.device("P1", P.HSG, parent=w1, contacts="DEMO-CRIMP-M")` |

## `d.terminal_strip`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tag` | required | The printed tag. `None` numbers the strip and needs `name=`. | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.TB, 10)` |
| `part` | required | The terminal part. `None` makes part-less terminals with only `.outer`, and needs `external=True`. | `d.terminal_strip("X9", None, external=True)` |
| `count` | `None` | The number of terminals. `X1[3]` takes terminal 3 and makes it on first use. | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.TB, count=10)` |
| `name` | `None` | The key a released number holds to. A floating strip, with `tag=None`, raises without it. | `d.terminal_strip(None, P.TB, name="field")` |
| `description` | `''` | Text for the strip in the designation list. Empty falls back to the part's. | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.TB, description="Field strip")` |
| `place` | `...` | Where the strip stands. See the `place=` table in `authoring.md`. | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.TB, place="HOLD")` |
| `pe` | `None` | The part of the strip's protective-earth terminals. A run labelled `"PE"` takes it, and raises without one. | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.TB, pe="DEMO-TB-PE-2.5")` |
| `interface` | `False` | Marks terminals as the unit's boundary: `True` marks all, a tuple of terminal numbers marks those. | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.TB, 4, interface=(1, 2))` |
| `unused` | `False` | Marks terminals as unused: `True` marks all, a tuple of terminal numbers marks those. | `d.terminal_strip("X1", P.TB, 4, unused=(3, 4))` |
| `bridged` | `False` | Bridges plain terminals with jumpers: `True` bridges all, `(first, last)` a range, a tuple of ranges several. | `d.terminal_strip("X4", P.TB, 6, bridged=(2, 6))` |
| `external` | `False` | `True` flags the strip and its terminals as supplied by others. | `d.terminal_strip("X9", P.TB, 4, external=True)` |

## `d.cable`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tag` | required | The printed tag. `None` numbers the cable and needs `name=`. | `d.cable("W1", P.CBL)` |
| `part` | required | The cable part. Its cores come from the part. | `d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5")` |
| `length_m` | `None` | The length in metres, stored as whole millimetres. It prints in the cable list. `None` leaves the length out. | `d.cable("W1", P.CBL, length_m=5)` |
| `place` | `...` | Where the cable stands. See the `place=` table in `authoring.md`. | `d.cable("W1", P.CBL, place="HOLD")` |
| `parent` | `None` | The harness that holds the cable. | `d.cable("W5", P.CBL, parent=h1)` |
| `name` | `None` | The key a released number holds to. A floating cable, with `tag=None`, raises without it. | `d.cable(None, P.CBL, name="motor-cable")` |
| `external` | `False` | `True` flags the cable as supplied by others. Its cores carry no flag. | `d.cable("W1", P.CBL, external=True)` |

## `d.add`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `definition` | required | The unit made by `fr.unit`. The call builds it as an instance and returns the unit function's result. | `u1 = d.add(board, "U1")` |
| `tag` | required | The instance's printed tag, bare and capitals. `None` numbers it from the unit's class code and needs `name=`. | `d.add(board, "U1")` |
| `place` | `...` | Where the instance stands. See the `place=` table in `authoring.md`. | `d.add(board, "U1", place="HOLD")` |
| `name` | `None` | The identity a released number holds to. A floating add raises without it. | `d.add(board, None, name="module1")` |
| `unused` | `()` | Names interface fields or functions the instance leaves unused, such as `"X1"` or `"X1.x1"`. | `d.add(board, "U1", unused=("X1.x1",))` |

## `d.ac_supply`

`d.ac_supply(name, voltage, *phases, ...)` takes the phase pins in phase order as `phases`: one or three.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | The supply's name. Its rails are `ac.L1` and so on. | `d.ac_supply("230V", 230, x0[1], n=x0[2])` |
| `voltage` | required | Each phase's RMS voltage to the star point. It is not read from a part. | `d.ac_supply("400V", 400, q1["L1"], q1["L2"], q1["L3"])` |
| `n` | `None` | The neutral pin. A series joins N only where an element has a pole for it. | `n=q1["N"]` |
| `names` | `None` | Renames the potentials: one name per phase pin in order, then one for `n`. The rails keep their `ac.L1` names. | `names=("A", "B", "C")` |
| `earthing` | `fr.EARTHED` | `fr.IT` declares a floating supply. | `earthing=fr.IT` |
| `fault_current_a` | `None` | The prospective fault current in amps, positive. The supply becomes a source for the breaking-capacity check. | `fault_current_a=10000` |

## `d.dc_supply`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | The supply's name. Its rails are `dc.plus` and `dc.minus`. | `d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)` |
| `source` | `None` | A device or function whose L+ and L- pins and nominal voltage are the supply. With none, `plus`, `minus` and `voltage` are required. | `d.dc_supply("24VDC", g1.output)` |
| `plus` | `None` | The plus pin, with no `source`. | `plus=x1[1]` |
| `minus` | `None` | The minus pin, with no `source`. | `minus=x1[2]` |
| `mid` | `None` | A middle conductor. With it, `mid` is 0 V and plus and minus are plus and minus the voltage. | `mid=x1[3]` |
| `voltage` | `None` | The voltage, required with no `source` or a source whose part states none. | `voltage=24` |
| `names` | `None` | Renames the potentials, in the order plus, minus, mid. | `names=("P24", "M24")` |
| `earthing` | `fr.EARTHED` | `fr.IT` declares a floating supply. | `earthing=fr.IT` |
| `fault_current_a` | `None` | The prospective fault current in amps, positive. A `source` refuses it, since the part states its own. | `fault_current_a=500` |
| `fault_time_constant_ms` | `None` | The fault time constant in milliseconds, positive. A `source` refuses it. | `fault_time_constant_ms=5` |

## `d.earth`

`d.earth(*pins)` takes the pins to join to protective earth, one `PE` net. It has no named keyword, and a terminal lands on its inner side. Example: `d.earth(x1[3], q1["PE"])`.

## `d.function`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | The function block's name, printed `=name`. The devices made inside the `with` block belong to it, which sets their designation; the `d.series` a function is written in sets where it draws. | `with d.function("RUN", "Pump run"):` |
| `text` | required | The block's description. It prints on the pages that draw the block. | `with d.function("RUN", "Pump run"):` |

## `d.location`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | The place's bare tag, printed `+name`. | `d.location("HOLD", "Engine hold")` |
| `text` | required | The place's description. | `d.location("HOLD", "Engine hold")` |
| `within` | `None` | The outer place, which must exist. The place then prints `+outer+name`. `None` puts it at the root. | `d.location("BATT", "Batteries", within="HOLD")` |

## `d.harness`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tag` | `None` | The part-less harness's printed tag. `None` numbers it and needs `name=`. | `d.harness("H1")` |
| `name` | `None` | The key a released number holds to. | `d.harness(None, name="main-loom")` |
| `place` | `...` | Where the harness stands. `None` gives it no place. See the `place=` table in `authoring.md`. | `d.harness("H1", place=None)` |
| `external` | `False` | `True` flags the harness as supplied by others. | `d.harness("H1", external=True)` |

## `d.rack`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tag` | required | The part-less PLC rack's printed tag. Modules go under it with `parent=`. | `d.rack("U1")` |
| `name` | `None` | The key a released number holds to. | `d.rack("U1", name="plc")` |
| `place` | `...` | Where the rack stands. `None` gives it no place. See the `place=` table in `authoring.md`. | `d.rack("U1", place="HOLD")` |
| `external` | `False` | `True` flags the rack as supplied by others. | `d.rack("U1", external=True)` |

## `d.mate`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a` | required | The connector to plug in: a device with one function, or that function. | `d.mate(j1, j2)` |
| `b` | required | The connector `a` plugs into. | `d.mate(j1, j2)` |

## `d.series`

`d.series(*elements, ...)` takes the elements to wire end to end, each one's load to the next one's line. A pin or a tuple of one device's pins starts or ends it (`keywords-handles.md`).

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wire` | `None` | The wire of every pole: a size, a table of rows that replaces only those rows, one `(colour, size)`, or a tuple of them, one per pole in pole order and as long as the series is wide. `None` uses the rows' defaults, and a row with no size is `WIRE_ROW_UNRESOLVED`. A series through a cable whose part has a core table needs no `wire=`. | `d.series(dc.plus, k1.aux, h1.lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))`; `d.series(x1[1:4], q1.element, wire=((BN, 1.5), (BK, 1.5), (GY, 1.5)))` |

## `d.pair`

`d.pair(a, cable, b)` joins two ends through a cable pin for pin: core `i` runs from `a`'s pin `i` to `b`'s pin `i`, with no line or load direction. It takes no keyword: the cores are the wires.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a` | required | The first end: terminals (`x8[1:3]`, their field side) or a function (`b1.sig`, its pins in connector order). | `x8[1:3]` |
| `cable` | required | The cable between the ends, from `d.cable`. | `w3` |
| `b` | required | The second end, with as many pins as `a`. A strip, a bare port or a device raises. | `b1.sig` |

Example: `d.pair(x8[1:3], w3, b1.sig)`.

## `d.parallel`

`d.parallel(*members)` takes the members to group, so a series puts each between the previous load and the next line. It has no named keyword and connects nothing alone. Example: `d.series(dc.plus, d.parallel(h1.lamp, h2.lamp), dc.minus)`.

## `d.poles`

`d.poles(*functions, ...)` takes one-pole contacts of one device, in pole order, as one element drawn multi-pole. It wires nothing: a series wires the group.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `selector` | `False` | `True` turns a changeover group's throws to the line side, so a series enters at the throws and leaves at the commons, and the group draws turned. `False` keeps the line at the commons. It raises on a part that already states a selector, and on a group that is not changeovers. | `q = d.poles(k1.co_1, k1.co_2, k1.co_3, selector=True)` |

## `d.project`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | required | The project title. It prints in every document's title block. | `d.project(title="Pump", ...)` |
| `number` | required | The drawing number, printed in the title block. | `number="DC-1"` |
| `customer` | required | The customer, printed in the title block. | `customer="Demo Ltd"` |
| `revision` | required | The current revision, an integer from 1. Its date is that of the matching `d.revision` entry. | `revision=2` |
| `author` | required | The author. A project document's Author cell prints it. | `author="AB"` |
| `notice` | `None` | Not accepted: passing it raises `AuthorError`. The notice moved to `fr.document(notice=)`. | `fr.document(preset, None, cover=c, notice="...")` |
| `version` | `1` | The project's release version. `d.revision` without `version=` writes entries of it. Set it before any `d.revision`. | `version=2` |

## `d.revision`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `revision` | required | The revision number of this history entry. | `d.revision(1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", created="AB")` |
| `date` | required | The entry's date. The title block shows it for the current revision. | `date="2026-01-01"` |
| `text` | required | What the revision changed. | `text="first issue"` |
| `created` | required | Who made the revision. | `created="AB"` |
| `checked` | `''` | Who checked it. Empty leaves the field empty. | `checked="CD"` |
| `approved` | `''` | Who approved it. Empty leaves the field empty. | `approved="EF"` |
| `version` | `None` | The version the entry belongs to. `None` takes the project's version, or 1 before `d.project`. | `version=2` |

## `d.rating`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `part` | required | A part class or MPN string. An MPN made by two makers raises. | `d.rating("DEMO-MCB-3P")` |
| `function` | `None` | A function template of the part. `None` reads the part's own rating. | `d.rating("DEMO-MCB-3P", "main")` |

## `d.operating`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `part` | required | A part class or MPN string. An MPN made by two makers raises. | `d.operating("DEMO-PSU-24", "output")` |
| `function` | required | The function template whose operating envelope is read. Returns `None` if the part states none. | `d.operating("DEMO-PSU-24", "output")` |

## `d.draft`

`d.draft()` takes nothing. It returns the records written so far, and it does not freeze them or merge the library: `fr.build` does both.

## `d.detail.wire`

`d.detail.wire(*pins, ...)` takes the pins to wire: two make one wire, more make a daisy chain.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wire` | `None` | The wire as `(colour, size)`, a size, or a table of rows, as `d.series` reads it, except a per-pole tuple. | `d.detail.wire(x1[1], h1[1], wire=(BU, 0.75))` |
| `label` | `None` | Text printed on the wire. `None` prints none. | `label="L1"` |
| `n` | `None` | `n=2` draws a second wire in parallel between the same two pins. `None` draws one. | `n=2` |

## `d.detail.star`

`d.detail.star(src, targets, ...)` wires `src` to each of `targets`, a tuple or list: one wire per target, none between targets.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `src` | required | The pin every wire starts at. A strip stands for one terminal, shared by all targets. | `d.detail.star(x2[17].outer, (x7[1], x7[4]))` |
| `targets` | required | A tuple or list of the pins to wire to. One target is `d.detail.wire(src, target)`. | `(x7[1], x7[4], x7[7])` |
| `wire` | `None` | The wire as `(colour, size)`, a size, or a table of rows, as `d.detail.wire` reads it. | `d.detail.star(x2[17].outer, (x7[1], x7[4]), wire=(BU, 0.75))` |

## `d.detail.net`

`d.detail.net(name, *pins, ...)` takes the pins the net spans as `pins`.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | The net's name. It prints on the net in the drawings and the wire list. | `d.detail.net("CAN", a[1], b[1])` |
| `kind` | `fr.CONTROL` | The `NetClass` of the net. It cannot make a `PE` or `POWER` net, which earth and supplies own. | `d.detail.net("CAN", a[1], b[1], kind=fr.SIGNAL)` |

## `d.detail.busbar`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a` | required | The first pin of the busbar, a conductor of kind `bus`. | `d.detail.busbar(x1[1], x1[2])` |
| `b` | required | The second pin. The same pin twice raises. | `d.detail.busbar(x1[1], x1[2])` |

## `d.detail.rail_bond`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a` | required | The first pin of the bond, a conductor of kind `rail`. | `d.detail.rail_bond(x1[1], x1[2])` |
| `b` | required | The second pin, of the same rail. The same pin twice raises. | `d.detail.rail_bond(x1[1], x1[2])` |

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/keywords-handles/index.md -->

# Keywords of the handle methods and layout hints

This page has one table for each handle method and each `d.layout.*` hint: each named keyword, its default, its effect and an example fragment.
A call that takes only `*args` has no table, and one sentence says what it takes.

The design calls are in `keywords-design.md`, the `fr.*` functions in `keywords-output.md`.
`d.layout.profile` and `d.layout.sheet` keep their tables in `layout-numbers.md`.

## `Fn.plc`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `signal` | required | The `fr.SignalType` of the PLC channel this function needs, such as `fr.DI`. It picks the channel kind allocated. | `k1.coil.plc(fr.DO, "pump-run")` |
| `name` | required | The channel's name. It prints in the PLC lists and on the channel's address. | `k1.coil.plc(fr.DO, "pump-run")` |
| `priority` | `0` | A lower number is served first when channels are short. Ties go by the requesting function's key, then its id. | `k1.coil.plc(fr.DO, "pump-run", priority=1)` |

## `Fn.pole`

`fn.pole(n)` takes one pole number, counted from 1 in pole order, and gives that one pole of the function as a series element: `d.series(s1.main.pole(2), f2.element, wire=(BK, 1.5))`.

A pin, or a tuple of one device's pins, is a series element at the start or the end only. First, its pins are the load ends: `d.series(k1.coil["A1"], a1.di_1, wire=(BK, 1.0))` leaves from A1, where `d.series(k1.coil, a1.di_1)` leaves from A2. Last, they are the line ends. In the middle a pin raises; use `d.detail.wire`.

`fn.pins` is the function's pins as a typed tuple in the connector list's order (`1, 2, 10, A1`): `a.pins[i]` is the i-th pin from 0, and a loop over it types as `fr.Pin`.

## `Fn.scale`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unit` | required | The engineering unit of the scaled value. It prints in the PLC list. | `ai.scale("bar", (0, 27648), (0, 10))` |
| `raw` | required | The raw range as two integers. | `raw=(0, 27648)` |
| `eng` | required | The engineering range as two strings or Decimals. Floats are refused. | `eng=("0", "10")` |

## `Fn.limits`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rating` | `None` | The rating the unit states about this boundary function. `None` states none. | `q1.line.limits(rating=r)` |
| `operating` | `None` | The operating envelope the unit states about this boundary function. `None` states none. | `q1.line.limits(operating=o)` |

## `Terminal.limits`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rating` | `None` | The rating the unit states about this terminal. `None` states none. The terminal must be in a unit. | `x1[1].limits(rating=r)` |
| `operating` | `None` | The operating envelope the unit states about this terminal. `None` states none. Giving neither value raises. | `x1[1].limits(operating=o)` |

## `TerminalStrip.run`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | required | The run's label. It prints on each terminal of the run. A run labelled `"PE"` takes the strip's `pe=` part. | `x1.run("24V", 4)` |
| `count` | `None` | The number of terminals in the run. With none, the run is bridged and grows as it is used. | `x1.run("24V", 4)` |
| `bridged` | `False` | Bridges the run's terminals with jumpers: `True` bridges all, `(first, last)` bridges a range. | `x1.run("24V", 4, bridged=True)` |
| `interface` | `False` | Marks the run's terminals as the unit's boundary: `True` marks all, a tuple of terminal numbers marks those. | `x1.run("24V", 4, interface=True)` |
| `unused` | `False` | Marks the run's terminals as unused: `True` marks all, a tuple marks those. | `x1.run("SPARE", 2, unused=True)` |

`TerminalStrip.label` is the strip's label as the design printed it (`"X5"`); `Run.label` is the run's own label (`"PE"`). Both are read-only.

## `Cable.core`

Use `d.series` through the cable first: it takes the next free core. Use `core` to choose one core.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `which` | required | The core, by colour or by 1-based number. | `w1.core(BN, a, b)` |
| `a` | required | The first pin of the core. With no `b`, the core is a shield core. | `w1.core(1, x1[1], m1["U"])` |
| `b` | `None` | The second pin of the core. `None` is for a shield core only. | `w1.core(BN, x1[1], m1["U"])` |

## `Cable.spare`

`Cable.spare(*cores, ...)` takes the cores to mark spare, by colour or number. With none, it marks every core not wired or marked so far, so wire first.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `at` | `None` | A pin that parks one spare core. `None` leaves it unparked. An `SH` core refuses it: use `core(which, a)`. | `w1.spare(BK, at=x1[9])` |

## `d.layout.break_before`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `group` | required | The function group that starts a new page. | `d.layout.break_before("pumps")` |

## `d.layout.chain`

`d.layout.chain(*functions, ...)` takes the functions to draw as one current path, source first.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `beside` | `None` | A host function: the chain is drawn next to it, joined at each end net it shares. It raises `AuthorError` when no end net is the host's. `None` draws the chain alone. | `d.layout.chain(a, b, beside=c)` |

## `d.layout.draw_in`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `function` | required | The function or device to draw in the group, whatever its device's place says. | `d.layout.draw_in(run, "pumps")` |
| `group` | required | The function group whose pages draw it. | `d.layout.draw_in(run, "pumps")` |

## `d.layout.keep_together`

`d.layout.keep_together(*groups)` takes the function groups that share a page when they fit. It has no named keyword. Example: `d.layout.keep_together("pumps", "valves")`.

## `d.layout.order`

`d.layout.order(*groups)` takes function groups: each neighbour pair is drawn in this order. It has no named keyword. Example: `d.layout.order("pumps", "valves")`.

## `d.layout.page_title`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `thing` | required | The group, function, device, strip or nested unit (what `d.add` returned) whose drawing pages get the title. One thing takes one title. | `d.layout.page_title("pumps", "Pump circuits")` |
| `text` | required | The title text. The page prints it before its blocks' texts. Empty raises `AuthorError`. | `d.layout.page_title("pumps", "Pump circuits")` |

## `d.layout.side`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target` | required | A field of a unit's interface, as `u1.bus_in`. An interface with no harness line ignores it. | `d.layout.side(f1, fr.ABOVE)` |
| `side` | required | `fr.ABOVE` or `fr.BELOW`: the edge the interface stands on. | `d.layout.side(f1, fr.BELOW)` |

## `d.layout.symbol`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target` | required | A function, a device, or a `FunctionKind` such as `FunctionKind.X`, passed as a name. A string raises. | `d.layout.symbol(P.Q, "breaker")` |
| `symbol` | required | The library symbol to draw. | `d.layout.symbol(P.Q, "breaker")` |
| `port_map` | `None` | Maps a model port name to a symbol port name where they differ. A port not listed keeps its name. These names are strings, the last place a typed part's pin is still one. | `port_map={"13": "1.in"}` |

## Keywords a consumer never passes

- `engine` on `Layout`: the design's engine. `d.layout` builds the layout around it, so you never pass it.
- `pe_mpn` on `TerminalStrip`: the strip's PE terminal part. Pass `pe=` to `d.terminal_strip` instead.

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.19.8/guide/keywords-output/index.md -->

# Keywords of the fr functions

This page has one table for each `fr.*` function: each named keyword, its default, its effect and an example call fragment.
A call that takes only `*args` has no table, and one sentence says what it takes.

The tier of each call is the first word of its docstring (index.md, Tiers).
The design calls are in `keywords-design.md`, the handle methods and layout hints in `keywords-handles.md`.

## `fr.design`

`fr.design(*libraries, ...)` takes the part libraries or generated parts modules as `libraries`.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `place` | `None` | Names the first location as a bare tag. With `None` the design has no location until you call `d.location`. | `fr.design("demo_parts", place="C1")` |
| `wiring` | `None` | Replaces the default wire colour and size of the rows it names, for this design. Rows not named keep the IEC 60204-1 default. | `fr.design("demo_parts", wiring={fr.DC_SUPPLY: (BU, 1.5)})` |

## `fr.unit`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | The unit release name. Instances print it, and the release folder under `fr.release` carries it. | `@fr.unit("pump-board", revision=2, ...)` |
| `revision` | required | The current revision. It is the last entry of the unit's history. | `revision=2` |
| `interface_version` | required | The unit's boundary version. You bump it by hand when the interface changes. | `interface_version=1` |
| `date` | required | Date of the current revision, as written in its history entry. | `date="2026-01-01"` |
| `text` | required | What the current revision changed, as written in its history entry. | `text="added the fuse"` |
| `by` | required | Who made the current revision. It prints in the history as `created`. | `by="AB"` |
| `version` | `1` | The release version. Revisions count within a version, and `fr.release` names the folder `<version>.<revision>`. | `version=2` |
| `title` | `''` | The unit's own title-block title. Empty gives a `TITLE_BLOCK_UNIT_IDENTITY_MISSING` warning on its document. | `title="Pump board"` |
| `number` | `''` | The unit's own title-block number. Empty gives a `TITLE_BLOCK_UNIT_IDENTITY_MISSING` warning on its document. | `number="DWG-101"` |
| `history` | `()` | Earlier revisions of the unit. Each entry is a mapping of the `d.revision` keywords `revision`, `date`, `text` and `created`. | `history=[{"revision": 1, "date": "2025-12-01", "text": "first", "created": "AB"}]` |
| `class_code` | `None` | One to three capital letters. A floating `d.add(fn, None, name=...)` numbers from this class. `None` gives no class, so a floating add raises. | `class_code="B"` |
| `wiring` | `None` | Replaces wire colour and size rows inside this unit's body only. A unit never takes its parent's rows. | `wiring={fr.DC_SUPPLY: (BU, 1.5)}` |

## `fr.document`

`fr.document(preset, subject, ...)` takes the preset and the subject as positional arguments.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `preset` | required | The `fr.DocumentPreset` that fixes the deliverable's default page kinds (documents.md). | `fr.document(fr.DocumentPreset.SYSTEM, None, cover=Path("cover.md"))` |
| `subject` | required | What the document is about: what `d.location(...)` returns, a `Device`, a unit release name, or `None` for the system preset. Another value raises `TypeError`. | `fr.document(preset, "pump-board", cover=cover)` |
| `cover` | required | The Markdown cover file, stored verbatim. Its stem is the document's key. A missing file raises `FileNotFoundError`. A `<stem>.notes.md` beside it becomes the notes page. | `cover=Path("cover.md")` |
| `add` | `()` | `fr.PageKind` values added to the preset's default pages. | `add=(fr.PageKind.OVERVIEW,)` |
| `remove` | `()` | `fr.PageKind` values removed from the preset's pages. | `remove=(fr.PageKind.NOTES,)` |
| `logo` | `None` | An SVG file for the title block's logo cell. `None` leaves the cell empty. A missing file raises. | `logo=Path("logo.svg")` |
| `notice` | `''` | The title block's IP notice text, printed on every page of this document. Empty leaves the cell empty. | `notice="Property of Demo Ltd"` |

## `fr.readability`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `result` | required | The `BuildResult` to measure. The layout runs again on its model, and the call returns one row per schematic page and one per unit. | `fr.readability(result)` |

## `fr.build`

`fr.build(*drafts, ...)` takes the drafts or `Design` objects to merge as `drafts`.

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `releases` | `None` | A release root. Numbering pins are seeded from the releases stored there, so a released unit keeps its numbers. `None` numbers freely. | `fr.build(d, releases=Path("releases"))` |

## `fr.check`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `result` | required | The `BuildResult` to check. Returns its findings plus the KiCad, PDF and render checks, errors first. | `fr.check(result)` |

## `fr.report`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `result` | required | The `BuildResult` to report. Returns one text: a summary line, each ERROR and WARNING with its fix, then counted notes. | `print(fr.report(result))` |

## `fr.write`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `result` | required | The built model whose exports are written. Any ERROR in `fr.check(result)` raises `BuildErrors` and writes nothing. | `fr.write(result, Path("out"))` |
| `out_dir` | required | The folder that receives the exports: the CSV reports, WAGO XML, overview and one PDF per document. | `fr.write(result, Path("out"))` |
| `unit` | `None` | Writes only that unit's own set, with no `overview.html`. `None` writes the whole model. | `fr.write(result, out, unit="pump-board")` |
| `intermediates` | `None` | A folder for SVGs, netlists and `.typ` sources. `None` keeps them in memory. | `intermediates=Path(".fransys")` |
| `releases` | `None` | A release root. With a stored release of the system there, `overview.html` marks what changed since it. `None` marks nothing. | `releases=Path("releases")` |

## `fr.export_names`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `result` | required | The `BuildResult`. Returns the file name `fr.write` gives each export, keyed by kind and subject. Writes nothing. | `fr.export_names(result)` |
| `unit` | `None` | Names only that unit's exports, as `fr.write(unit=)` would. `None` names the whole model's. | `fr.export_names(result, unit="pump-board")` |

## `fr.release`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `result` | required | The built model to release. Any ERROR raises `BuildErrors` and writes nothing. | `fr.release(result, Path("releases"))` |
| `into` | required | The release root. The call writes `<into>/<name>/<version>.<revision>/`. An identical stored listing returns the existing path. | `fr.release(result, Path("releases"))` |
| `unit` | `None` | Releases that unit instead of the system. | `fr.release(result, into, unit="pump-board")` |

## `fr.releases`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `root` | required | The release root to read. Returns each release folder in name, version, revision order. A missing root gives `()`. | `fr.releases(Path("releases"))` |

## `fr.diff`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `result` | required | The built model to compare. Returns the Markdown change list against a stored release. | `fr.diff(result, Path("releases"))` |
| `baselines` | required | The release root that holds the stored release. A missing release raises `FileNotFoundError`. | `fr.diff(result, Path("releases"))` |
| `unit` | `None` | Compares that unit instead of the system. | `fr.diff(result, root, unit="pump-board")` |
| `against` | `None` | A `<version>.<revision>` folder to compare with. `None` takes the release at the model's revision, else the previous one. | `against="1.3"` |

## `fr.verify`

| keyword | default | effect | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `result` | required | The rebuilt model. Returns one `BASELINE_DIFFERS` ERROR per unit instance, or the system, whose listing digest drifted. | `fr.verify(result, Path("releases"))` |
| `baselines` | required | The release root with the stored baselines. A unit with no stored baseline is not reported. | `fr.verify(result, Path("releases"))` |

## `fr.parts`

`fr.parts(*packages)` takes part-data package import names. It has no named keyword and returns one `Draft`. Zero names give an empty `Draft`. Example: `fr.parts("demo_parts")`.

## `fr.parts_module`

`fr.parts_module(*sources)` takes the library names to generate a typed parts module for. It has no named keyword and returns the module's text. Example: `fr.parts_module("demo_parts")`.

## `fr.lint`

`fr.lint(*libraries)` takes part-library import names. It has no named keyword and returns their findings, library by library. Zero libraries give `()`. Example: `fr.lint("demo_parts")`.
